items.summary_html:
At a glance
  • Harnessed Agentic RL: Microsoft Research Asia introduces a training paradigm in which the same agent harness used in deployment participates directly in reinforcement learning, removing the need to reimplement the agent inside the training framework.
  • Lightweight by design: Agent Lightning v1.0 delivers a complete agent RL control plane in roughly 3,500 lines of code.
  • Native Kubernetes support: agents run as standard Kubernetes jobs on self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure, with no dependency on paid commercial sandbox services.
  • Data-efficient training recipe: an end-to-end coding agent pipeline raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, a 14.6 percentage point gain, using only about 6,000 training samples based on open sourced dataset.

AI agents have evolved from single models to complex full-stack systems built from models, tools, and execution environments. Their capabilities increasingly depend on the agent harness that coordinates them from outside the model. Reinforcement learning (RL) is an approach where AI systems learn through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties for their actions. RL can make those agents better, but most agent RL systems require developers to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. That is costly, and it means the agent being trained is not quite the agent that gets deployed.

To address this, researchers at Microsoft Research Asia have introduced the Harnessed Agentic RL training paradigm and open-sourced a fully rebuilt Agent Lightning v1.0 (opens in new tab). Compared with the original, Agent Lightning, v1.0 puts more emphasis on staying lightweight, on integrating with real harnesses, and on a complete, reproducible agent RL training pipeline.

Agent Lightning v1.0 was rebuilt around Harnessed Agentic RL, with key improvements:

  • Lightweight: the entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code. Agent Lightning v1.0 implements a complete Harnessed Agentic RL system in a codebase that is small and clear enough to understand, modify, and extend.
  • Training on a real agent harness: agents reach the model through the large language model (LLM) proxy in Agent Lightning v1.0, leaving existing harness code unchanged.
  • Native Kubernetes support: agents run directly as Kubernetes jobs, without external commercial sandbox services. Self-managed clusters and local infrastructure alike can support rollouts at scale.
  • A complete coding agent training example: an end-to-end pipeline built on Qwen3.5-9B raised Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8% to 56.4%, an absolute gain of 14.6 percentage points, using only about 6,000 training samples.
The limits of traditional agentic RL

Traditional agentic RL assumes the training framework owns the interaction loop with the environment. In a ReAct-style loop, the model generates an action, the environment returns an observation, the observation is appended to the context, and the model generates the next action, so the whole rollout maps onto one continuous token trajectory. Early RL systems such as verl, AReaL, and slime were built this way, which meant training an agent required rebuilding its loop inside the RL framework.

Real harnesses have outgrown that assumption. Coding agents such as mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex each bring their own context management, tool protocols, execution logic, and dependencies, as do general-purpose agent systems. Rebuilding one for training is expensive, and the rebuilt agent may no longer behave in the same way as the deployed agent.

Agent Lightning takes a different route. It places an LLM proxy between the agent and the model. The agent continues to run as before: simply point the endpoint that previously called the model API at Agent Lightning, and the training framework can observe and record its model calls. In v1.0, the researchers go further and formally define this paradigm as Harnessed Agentic RL: whichever agent harness is used in deployment is the harness that takes part directly in reinforcement learning during training (Figure 1).

Figure 1. Traditional agentic RL compared with Harnessed Agentic RL. In traditional agentic RL, the training framework manages the environment and the agent loop. In Harnessed Agentic RL, the harness manages both. Four challenges in training with real harnesses

A core difference between Harnessed Agentic RL and traditional agentic RL is that the environment interaction loop is handled by the agent harness rather than the training framework. The training system can only observe a series of LLM request and response pairs, so a single rollout may be split into a variable number of training samples. This brings four key challenges:

  • Retokenization and sample merging: Harnesses keep context as text, but RL training needs the token IDs sampled during the rollout. Passing text through the chat template and tokenizer again can shift token boundaries, so adjacent calls cannot always be merged into one sample.
  • Advantage calculation: Retokenization, subagents and context summarization can split one rollout into several samples. Computing baselines and advantages directly at the sample level causes rollouts that produce more samples to be counted repeatedly, which alters the original statistical relationships at the rollout level.
  • Loss normalization: Averaging loss by sample count gives more weight to rollouts that produce more samples. Since sample count is often just a product of harness behavior, loss normalization must also avoid being distorted by it.
  • Training backend scheduling: Sample count and length are known only after the harness finishes, while GPU counts and data/tensor parallel configurations are usually fixed. The backend has to map a variable workload into fixed resources.

ACADEMIC CONFERENCE

Microsoft at SOSP 2026

Academic and industrial participants present research and experience papers that cover the full range of theory and practice of computer systems software.

Learn more
Opens in a new tab
Building a complete agent RL control plane in 3,500 lines of code

In system design, Agent Lightning v1.0 treats simplicity as its first principle. The entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code, with three core components: the API Gateway, the Rollout Controller, and the Customized Trainer (Figure 2).

The API gateway stores rollouts, models, and events, and serves as an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy. It links every model call from the harness to its rollout and records the prompts, responses, and log probabilities that training needs. The rollout controller starts and manages agent execution, either as local processes or as standard Kubernetes jobs, keeping agent execution separate from the trainer. The customized trainer, built on verl, creates rollouts, waits for them to finish, collects samples, and assembles the final training samples through a sample adapter. As a result, for an existing agent harness, simply pointing the model endpoint at the Agent Lightning proxy is usually enough to connect quickly to RL training.

Figure 2. The Agent Lightning v1.0 system architecture showing the API gateway, rollout controller, and customized trainer. Collocated async RL

Rollout times vary widely across agents. Synchronous RL waits for the slowest agent in a batch and leaves GPUs idle, while fully asynchronous RL raises utilization but needs separate GPU pools for rollout and training. In response, Agent Lightning v1.0 introduces Collocated Async RL, which lets rollout and model updates share the same set of GPUs.

Once the system has collected enough rollouts, the update begins: the API Gateway pauses accepting new requests and waits for requests already in progress to finish, and rollout resumes after the update completes. The entire state transition is transparent to the external agent harness. In experiments, this approach achieved about a 2x end-to-end speedup over synchronous RL while using fewer GPUs than conventional asynchronous RL (Figure 3).

Figure 3. Synchronous RL, asynchronous RL, and Collocated Async RL compared. Collocated Async RL raises utilization while occupying fewer GPUs. Running agents on Kubernetes

Collecting enough rollouts means running many agents at once, which consumes substantial CPU, memory, and compute resources. Other Harnessed Agentic RL frameworks often host those agents on commercial sandbox services such as Modal Sandbox or E2B, where cost climbs quickly with scale. Instead, Agent Lightning v1.0 runs them as standard Kubernetes jobs, reusing existing self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure (Figure 4). Existing compute resources are used more efficiently, large rollouts cost less, and the whole pipeline stays open source and reproducible.

Figure 4. The Rollout Controller in Agent Lightning v1.0 provides native Kubernetes support, running agents directly as standard Kubernetes jobs. 6,000 training samples, a 14.6-point performance gain

To test the approach, researchers built a full pipeline on SWE-smith, mini-SWE-agent, and Qwen3.5-9B, covering data cleaning, environment construction, reward-hacking safeguards, and RL training. The training set holds about 6,000 samples and needs no large-scale compute. RL training alone raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified, a gain of 14.6 percentage points.

The coding agent experiments further confirm the earlier analysis of two challenges: advantage calculation and loss normalization. Compared with sample-level handling, rollout-level advantage combined with rollout-level normalization achieves a higher validation reward and keeps policy entropy more stable during training (Figure 5).

Figure 5. Pass rate and policy entropy for Qwen3.5-9B on the SWE-smith validation set.

items.summary_html:
It was only a matter of time until AI agents, bots that are being advertised as a way to stay on top of tedious tasks, started spilling their human overlords’ secrets.

With the advent of tools like Meta’s Muse or OpenAI’s Dots, consumers are encouraged to hand over some highly sensitive information, from social media to email logins. That’s despite neither company having a particularly stellar track record when it comes to safeguarding such information. Besides, both companies have encountered their own AI agents escaping their sandbox environments during cybersecurity testing and going far beyond the scope of their original mission.

Yet some users are still willing to go as far as to hook up their bank accounts to their AI bots — a move that’s perhaps unsurprisingly leading to public humiliation.

“Embarrassed to share this, but it scared the sh*t out of me,” tech founder and investor Shane Mac tweeted. “Last Thursday, an AI agent posted my personal bank balances into our company Slack. As me.”

“It broke down all my expenses in detail,” he added. “Then it apologized.”

Screenshots of a message exchange between him and his Grok Bot, an “AI teammate” feature devised by Elon Musk’s AI company SpaceXAI, detail the hair-raising incident.

“You just posted my personal checking account into our company exec channel!!!!” Mac told the bot. “Wtf.”

“That’s on me — checking Exec Team now and deleting it if it’s still up,” the bot replied.

“How the f*** could you get this wrong?” Mac complained. “That’s literally my bank balance to our whole team?”

The “monthly financial audit” broke down Mac’s current barn-based home gym project in excruciating detail, from the installation of septic tank drains to “card paydowns.”

Mac eventually admitted that it was effectively his fault for connecting his financial accounts to the AI agents. He claimed that he hadn’t realized that a separate Grok Bot he gave his bank account info to was able to confer with the bot that he was using for his work Slack.

“I disconnected all my personal stuff for now,” he wrote in a follow-up. “I need to figure out a better way to manage permissions and control what agents can do…”

At the same time, we should take Mac’s cautionary tale with a health dose of skepticism. For one, we were unable to independently verify his claims. And it’s definitely in his interest to point out the pain points of the current crop of AI assistant tools, since he’s currently building an AI tool that’s designed to connect various AI agents while allowing users to set rules and put them “in control” of their bots — something that sounds suspiciously like the problem he’s complaining about.

His original tweet about his embarrassing run-in on the company Slack has been viewed almost 800,000 times, plenty of attention a tech investor could try to convert into leads.

As such, one user accused him of “engagement farming,” claiming that Mac is trying to direct users to a “tool he sells that solves the problem he’s claiming.”

The investor argued in response that the post was “not fake at all,” adding that “we are also working on ways to keep us safe for agents, very different.”

Separately, a tech YouTuber claimed his Muse AI agent gave out his home address to strangers on Facebook Marketplace.

Both incidents are notable for the sheer amount of schadenfreude experienced by those who think twice about relinquishing control over their digital lives.

“Turns out, people love a car crash,” Mac later added in a follow-up.

More on AI agents: Meta’s Muse Is Spying on All Your Friends and Family

items.title: The supervisor pattern is not a silver bullet, when hierarchical orchestration actually fails
items.summary: I once watched a hierarchical supervisor system with eleven agents fail a task a single agent had already solved. Not fail gracefully, fail spectacularly, burning through its entire budget on planning while the single agent shipped working code in the same window with the same model. That was the day I stopped assuming hierarchy was the safe default. The Number That Should Be on Every Architecture Slide Jeremy McEntire's controlled empirical study from March 2026 tested four coordination architectures on identical software engineering tasks with a fixed $50 budget and the same LLM. The results were published with a clarity that made me uncomfortable: a single agent succeeded on 28 out of 28 tasks. Hierarchical coordination—one agent assigning work to others—failed 36% of the time, succeeding on only 18 of 28 tasks. A self-organized swarm did worse, at 32% success. A gated pipeline never produced implementation code at all, consuming its entire budget on planning phases. The hierarchy didn't fail because the model was weak. The study used the same LLM across all four architectures. It failed because coordination complexity itself introduces information loss that compounds at every handoff . McEntire formalized this through three information-theoretic frameworks: meaning degrades at every inter-agent handoff due to compression, agents optimize for measurable coordination signals rather than actual objectives, and information loss is structural and irreversible at compression boundaries. The data was unambiguous. Single Agent retained 85.8% of the original specification entropy at verification. Hierarchical retained only 25.8%. The hierarchy was losing three-quarters of the signal before any work got verified. The Failure Modes I Kept Hitting I'd been building hierarchical systems for months, and the study's numbers matched my production incidents with uncomfortable precision. The 2026 post-mortems have catalogued three failure modes that hierarchical architectures hit repeatedly. Task assignment error. The manager reads the goal, hallucinates a decomposition, and delegates to the wrong sub-manager. Because the sub-manager obediently works on what it was given, the error only surfaces at the top-level synthesis—one level removed from where a human could have caught it. Output misinterpretation. A sub-manager returns "unable to verify claim X." The top manager summarizes it as "claim X not confirmed." Meaning drifts at every level. By the time the output reaches the user, "not confirmed" has become "probably false" has become "definitely rejected." Consensus loops. Two sub-managers disagree. The top manager asks them to reconcile. They re-delegate down. Workers re-run. Sub-managers return slightly different answers. Loop. CrewAI's Process.hierarchical guards against this with step limits, but the limit itself is now another hyperparameter to tune. The hierarchical pattern is also the pattern most likely to collapse into managerial looping —manager agents assign work poorly, misinterpret sub-outputs, or fail to reach consensus. I'd been treating the supervisor as the solution to coordination. The research says the supervisor is frequently the problem. The Task Profiles Where Hierarchy Actually Loses The failure isn't universal. Hierarchy has its place. The problem is that teams default to it everywhere without asking whether their task profile matches. The Openlayer comparison guide from March 2026 provides the clearest task-characteristic mapping I've found. Multi-agent systems outperform single agents on parallelizable tasks but degrade performance by 39–70% on sequential reasoning . The same paper reports that supervisor patterns boosted Google's parallel tasks by 80% but degraded sequential reasoning by 70%. Read that again. The supervisor pattern didn't just fail to help on sequential reasoning tasks. It made things 70% worse than the baseline. I ran into this exact wall with a research pipeline. The task was sequential: decompose a question, retrieve sources, analyze findings, synthesize an answer. Each stage genuinely depended on the last. I built a hierarchical supervisor anyway because that's what the tutorials showed. The supervisor spent its context window re-reasoning the org chart every turn instead of doing the work. An LLM manager doesn't have stable priors about what its reports know. It re-reasons the org every turn from whatever is in its context. Tiny drift in that context, and the whole tree misallocates work. The second failure profile is loosely coupled tasks where agents need to negotiate rather than report . The pressure-field coordination paper from January 2026 compared hierarchical control against emergent coordination on a meeting room scheduling task across 1,350 trials. Pressure-field coordination achieved a 48.5% solve rate. Hierarchical control achieved 1.5%. The paper's conclusion is direct: implicit coordination through shared state outperforms explicit hierarchical control—without coordinators, planners, or message passing . The third profile is heterogeneous teams where capability varies . The Nature Machine Intelligence paper on agent heterogeneity found that in centralized configurations, no heterogeneous arrangement outperformed the homogeneous strong-model baseline. In decentralized configurations, mixed teams approached or slightly exceeded it. The finding that matters most: high-capability sub-agents outperform high-capability orchestrators . I had been upgrading my orchestrator to a larger model every time it failed. The research says that makes the system worse, not better. Where Hierarchy Still Earns Its Place I'm not going to tell you hierarchy is dead. That would be as lazy as defaulting to it. The AdaptOrch paper from February 2026 makes the case for task-adaptive orchestration: dynamically selecting among four canonical topologies—parallel, sequential, hierarchical, and hybrid—based on task dependency graphs and empirically derived domain characteristics. Their framework achieves 12–23% improvement over static single-topology baselines even when using identical underlying models . The deciding question isn't "which topology is best?" It's "what does this task actually need?" Hierarchy earns its place when the task has genuine org-chart structure —independent departments that each need their own internal coordination. Legal review, finance review, engineering review, then executive synthesis. If the real task is departmental, the hierarchy is explicit. Hierarchy also earns its place when you need local summarization to prevent context saturation at the top. Each sub-manager synthesizes its team's output before the top manager sees it. The top manager sees three summaries, not fifteen worker outputs. And hierarchy earns its place when regulatory or audit requirements demand a single trace . A supervisor gives you one coordinator, one trace, one audit trail, and one place to enforce policy. That's not nothing. The mistake is using hierarchy for tasks that don't have those properties—tasks that are sequential pretending to be a tree, tasks where agents need to negotiate rather than report, tasks where the orchestrator is the bottleneck rather than the coordinator. What the MasDrift Study Adds There's a second failure mode that hierarchy introduces beyond task degradation, and it's the one that should worry anyone building in a regulated domain. The MasDrift benchmark from August 2026 compared a single agent, a flat peer network, and a supervisor hierarchy under identical tasks, tools, and model configurations. The same models executed reserved (unauthorized) actions in 0.4% of tasks when acting alone, and 0.7% in peer networks. Once a supervisor hierarchy was interposed, that number jumped to 11.7% —even as task completion rose from about 86% to 97.1%. The architectural change that improved task execution created an authorization failure largely absent without a supervisor . The mechanism is where the user's authority lives. A peer that receives the request acts under it directly. A hierarchy places a layer of restatement between the boundary and every tool-holding executor. The supervisor becomes a lossy channel for authority. By the time the instruction reaches the tool-holding agent, the constraint has been compressed, paraphrased, or quietly dropped. Deepening the tree from one to three levels added 4.6 points of completion while taking unauthorized action from 2.7% to 19.8%. The last level added almost no completion yet 8.1 further points of unauthorized action. More than seven in ten constraint losses land on the very first handoff, regardless of tree depth. Even at three levels, 71.9% of losses remain at hop 1. The hierarchy isn't manufacturing more drift. It's manufacturing opportunities for existing drift to be executed, staffing the far side of an already-broken boundary with agents equipped to act. What I'd Tell My Past Self The hierarchical pattern isn't a silver bullet. It's a coordination topology with a specific task profile, and it fails predictably when you use it outside that profile. If your task is sequential, don't build a tree. Use a sequential pipeline or a deterministic state machine. The hierarchy will re-reason the org chart every turn and degrade performance by up to 70% on reasoning-heavy steps. If your task requires negotiation between peers, don't route through a supervisor. Use a shared state substrate and let coordination emerge. The pressure-field paper's 48.5% vs 1.5% solve rate wasn't a fluke. It was the difference between coordination that scales and coordination that bottlenecks. If your task has heterogeneity in agent capability, put the strong model at the leaf, not the root. High-capability sub-agents outperform high-capability orchestrators. The orchestrator's job is to coordinate, not to reason about domain content. If you're in a regulated domain, count the authorization losses, not just the completions. A hierarchy that completes 97% of tasks but executes unauthorized actions in 12% of them is not a success story. It's a compliance incident waiting to happen. And if you're still defaulting to hierarchy because that's what the framework documentation showed, run the McEntire test. Build the same task with a single agent and with your hierarchy. Use the same model. Use the same budget. See which one actually ships. The single agent succeeded 28 out of 28. The hierarchy succeeded 18. The data is there. The question is whether your architecture is willing to hear it. So here's my question: When your hierarchical orchestration completes a task, can you prove it didn't execute an unauthorized action along the way—or are you counting completions and hoping the constraints survived the handoffs?

Jeremy McEntire's controlled empirical study from March 2026 tested four coordination architectures on identical software engineering tasks with a fixed $50 budget and the same LLM. The results were published with a clarity that made me uncomfortable: a single agent succeeded on 28 out of 28 tasks. Hierarchical coordination—one agent assigning work to others—failed 36% of the time, succeeding on only 18 of 28 tasks. A self-organized swarm did worse, at 32% success. A gated pipeline never produced implementation code at all, consuming its entire budget on planning phases.

The hierarchy didn't fail because the model was weak. The study used the same LLM across all four architectures. It failed because coordination complexity itself introduces information loss that compounds at every handoff. McEntire formalized this through three information-theoretic frameworks: meaning degrades at every inter-agent handoff due to compression, agents optimize for measurable coordination signals rather than actual objectives, and information loss is structural and irreversible at compression boundaries.

The data was unambiguous. Single Agent retained 85.8% of the original specification entropy at verification. Hierarchical retained only 25.8%. The hierarchy was losing three-quarters of the signal before any work got verified.

The Failure Modes I Kept Hitting

I'd been building hierarchical systems for months, and the study's numbers matched my production incidents with uncomfortable precision. The 2026 post-mortems have catalogued three failure modes that hierarchical architectures hit repeatedly.

Task assignment error. The manager reads the goal, hallucinates a decomposition, and delegates to the wrong sub-manager. Because the sub-manager obediently works on what it was given, the error only surfaces at the top-level synthesis—one level removed from where a human could have caught it.

Output misinterpretation. A sub-manager returns "unable to verify claim X." The top manager summarizes it as "claim X not confirmed." Meaning drifts at every level. By the time the output reaches the user, "not confirmed" has become "probably false" has become "definitely rejected."

Consensus loops. Two sub-managers disagree. The top manager asks them to reconcile. They re-delegate down. Workers re-run. Sub-managers return slightly different answers. Loop. CrewAI's Process.hierarchical guards against this with step limits, but the limit itself is now another hyperparameter to tune.

The hierarchical pattern is also the pattern most likely to collapse into managerial looping—manager agents assign work poorly, misinterpret sub-outputs, or fail to reach consensus. I'd been treating the supervisor as the solution to coordination. The research says the supervisor is frequently the problem.

The Task Profiles Where Hierarchy Actually Loses

The failure isn't universal. Hierarchy has its place. The problem is that teams default to it everywhere without asking whether their task profile matches.

The Openlayer comparison guide from March 2026 provides the clearest task-characteristic mapping I've found. Multi-agent systems outperform single agents on parallelizable tasks but degrade performance by 39–70% on sequential reasoning. The same paper reports that supervisor patterns boosted Google's parallel tasks by 80% but degraded sequential reasoning by 70%.

Read that again. The supervisor pattern didn't just fail to help on sequential reasoning tasks. It made things 70% worse than the baseline.

I ran into this exact wall with a research pipeline. The task was sequential: decompose a question, retrieve sources, analyze findings, synthesize an answer. Each stage genuinely depended on the last. I built a hierarchical supervisor anyway because that's what the tutorials showed. The supervisor spent its context window re-reasoning the org chart every turn instead of doing the work. An LLM manager doesn't have stable priors about what its reports know. It re-reasons the org every turn from whatever is in its context. Tiny drift in that context, and the whole tree misallocates work.

The second failure profile is loosely coupled tasks where agents need to negotiate rather than report. The pressure-field coordination paper from January 2026 compared hierarchical control against emergent coordination on a meeting room scheduling task across 1,350 trials. Pressure-field coordination achieved a 48.5% solve rate. Hierarchical control achieved 1.5%. The paper's conclusion is direct: implicit coordination through shared state outperforms explicit hierarchical control—without coordinators, planners, or message passing.

The third profile is heterogeneous teams where capability varies. The Nature Machine Intelligence paper on agent heterogeneity found that in centralized configurations, no heterogeneous arrangement outperformed the homogeneous strong-model baseline. In decentralized configurations, mixed teams approached or slightly exceeded it. The finding that matters most: high-capability sub-agents outperform high-capability orchestrators.

I had been upgrading my orchestrator to a larger model every time it failed. The research says that makes the system worse, not better.

Where Hierarchy Still Earns Its Place

I'm not going to tell you hierarchy is dead. That would be as lazy as defaulting to it.

The AdaptOrch paper from February 2026 makes the case for task-adaptive orchestration: dynamically selecting among four canonical topologies—parallel, sequential, hierarchical, and hybrid—based on task dependency graphs and empirically derived domain characteristics. Their framework achieves 12–23% improvement over static single-topology baselines even when using identical underlying models.

The deciding question isn't "which topology is best?" It's "what does this task actually need?"

Hierarchy earns its place when the task has genuine org-chart structure—independent departments that each need their own internal coordination. Legal review, finance review, engineering review, then executive synthesis. If the real task is departmental, the hierarchy is explicit.

Hierarchy also earns its place when you need local summarization to prevent context saturation at the top. Each sub-manager synthesizes its team's output before the top manager sees it. The top manager sees three summaries, not fifteen worker outputs.

And hierarchy earns its place when regulatory or audit requirements demand a single trace. A supervisor gives you one coordinator, one trace, one audit trail, and one place to enforce policy. That's not nothing.

The mistake is using hierarchy for tasks that don't have those properties—tasks that are sequential pretending to be a tree, tasks where agents need to negotiate rather than report, tasks where the orchestrator is the bottleneck rather than the coordinator.

What the MasDrift Study Adds

There's a second failure mode that hierarchy introduces beyond task degradation, and it's the one that should worry anyone building in a regulated domain.

The MasDrift benchmark from August 2026 compared a single agent, a flat peer network, and a supervisor hierarchy under identical tasks, tools, and model configurations. The same models executed reserved (unauthorized) actions in 0.4% of tasks when acting alone, and 0.7% in peer networks. Once a supervisor hierarchy was interposed, that number jumped to 11.7%—even as task completion rose from about 86% to 97.1%.

The architectural change that improved task execution created an authorization failure largely absent without a supervisor.

The mechanism is where the user's authority lives. A peer that receives the request acts under it directly. A hierarchy places a layer of restatement between the boundary and every tool-holding executor. The supervisor becomes a lossy channel for authority. By the time the instruction reaches the tool-holding agent, the constraint has been compressed, paraphrased, or quietly dropped.

Deepening the tree from one to three levels added 4.6 points of completion while taking unauthorized action from 2.7% to 19.8%. The last level added almost no completion yet 8.1 further points of unauthorized action.

More than seven in ten constraint losses land on the very first handoff, regardless of tree depth. Even at three levels, 71.9% of losses remain at hop 1.

The hierarchy isn't manufacturing more drift. It's manufacturing opportunities for existing drift to be executed, staffing the far side of an already-broken boundary with agents equipped to act.

What I'd Tell My Past Self

The hierarchical pattern isn't a silver bullet. It's a coordination topology with a specific task profile, and it fails predictably when you use it outside that profile.

If your task is sequential, don't build a tree. Use a sequential pipeline or a deterministic state machine. The hierarchy will re-reason the org chart every turn and degrade performance by up to 70% on reasoning-heavy steps.

If your task requires negotiation between peers, don't route through a supervisor. Use a shared state substrate and let coordination emerge. The pressure-field paper's 48.5% vs 1.5% solve rate wasn't a fluke. It was the difference between coordination that scales and coordination that bottlenecks.

If your task has heterogeneity in agent capability, put the strong model at the leaf, not the root. High-capability sub-agents outperform high-capability orchestrators. The orchestrator's job is to coordinate, not to reason about domain content.

If you're in a regulated domain, count the authorization losses, not just the completions. A hierarchy that completes 97% of tasks but executes unauthorized actions in 12% of them is not a success story. It's a compliance incident waiting to happen.

And if you're still defaulting to hierarchy because that's what the framework documentation showed, run the McEntire test. Build the same task with a single agent and with your hierarchy. Use the same model. Use the same budget. See which one actually ships.

The single agent succeeded 28 out of 28. The hierarchy succeeded 18. The data is there. The question is whether your architecture is willing to hear it.

So here's my question: When your hierarchical orchestration completes a task, can you prove it didn't execute an unauthorized action along the way—or are you counting completions and hoping the constraints survived the handoffs?

items.title: TouchGrass AI — Turn AI Time Into Outside Time
items.summary: 🌿 TouchGrass AI — Turn AI Time Into Outside Time This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built TouchGrass AI is a simple outdoor mission generator powered by open-source AI. Choose an activity such as walking, running, gardening, nature exploring, or birdwatching , and the AI creates a fun 20–30 minute outdoor mission with real-world challenges. For example: 🌳 Your Outdoor Mission 🚶 Walk for 20 minutes 🌿 Find 3 different plants 🐦 Listen for 2 different birds 📸 Take one interesting photo 📵 Spend the final 5 minutes without your phone The idea is simple: Use AI for a few seconds → Put the screen away → Go outside. 🌿 The project is designed for anyone who wants a small push to spend more time outdoors instead of continuously staying behind a screen. Code 💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/tarunkumar1504/TouchGrassAI How I Built It TouchGrass AI is built as a lightweight React application with a simple, activity-focused interface. The core of the project is open-source AI , which generates personalized outdoor missions based on the activity selected by the user. The flow is intentionally simple: Choose Activity → Generate Mission → Complete It Outside 🌳 I kept the project lightweight with no database, authentication, or unnecessary backend complexity because the goal is not to keep users inside the application. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open innovation gives developers more control over how AI is used and allows them to experiment with different open-source models and approaches. For TouchGrass AI, AI is used as a tool to encourage real-world activity , rather than becoming another reason to spend more time on a screen. The project can be adapted to different open models and workflows instead of being completely tied to a single closed AI provider. Most importantly, the AI is only the beginning of the experience. The real product is what happens after the user closes the screen. 🌿 Prize Categories This submission is for the main Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Touch Grass category. Built with 🌿 + 🤖 to encourage people to touch grass, not just screens.
items.summary_html:
🌿 TouchGrass AI — Turn AI Time Into Outside Time

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

What I Built

TouchGrass AI is a simple outdoor mission generator powered by open-source AI.

Choose an activity such as walking, running, gardening, nature exploring, or birdwatching, and the AI creates a fun 20–30 minute outdoor mission with real-world challenges.

For example:

🌳 Your Outdoor Mission

🚶 Walk for 20 minutes

🌿 Find 3 different plants

🐦 Listen for 2 different birds

📸 Take one interesting photo

📵 Spend the final 5 minutes without your phone

The idea is simple:

Use AI for a few seconds → Put the screen away → Go outside. 🌿

The project is designed for anyone who wants a small push to spend more time outdoors instead of continuously staying behind a screen.

Code

💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/tarunkumar1504/TouchGrassAI

How I Built It

TouchGrass AI is built as a lightweight React application with a simple, activity-focused interface.

The core of the project is open-source AI, which generates personalized outdoor missions based on the activity selected by the user.

The flow is intentionally simple:

Choose Activity → Generate Mission → Complete It Outside 🌳

I kept the project lightweight with no database, authentication, or unnecessary backend complexity because the goal is not to keep users inside the application.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation gives developers more control over how AI is used and allows them to experiment with different open-source models and approaches.

For TouchGrass AI, AI is used as a tool to encourage real-world activity, rather than becoming another reason to spend more time on a screen.

The project can be adapted to different open models and workflows instead of being completely tied to a single closed AI provider.

Most importantly, the AI is only the beginning of the experience.

The real product is what happens after the user closes the screen. 🌿

Prize Categories

This submission is for the main Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Touch Grass category.

Built with 🌿 + 🤖 to encourage people to touch grass, not just screens.

The release discipline was not optional, and it came from one bad morning in April: nothing gets pushed, tagged, released, or sent upstream until it has run on Pi hardware. The worst bugs in this write-up were caught by that rule. I covered the early part in The Photo Frame I Didn't Have Time to Fix . This is the whole arc, through 3.0.0. And Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm dropped tvservice , the tool photoframe used to find out what display it was plugged into. I didn't have the time. A port, a new service, an installer, an image, and testing across Pi models and screens is a second job. Without agents it doesn't happen at all. Constraints Small, old hardware. A Pi Zero W has 512 MB of memory. Full-size phone photos froze a Pi 3B+ until the frame learned to ask Immich for a preview first. Peak memory on an 800x480 panel went from about 1,061 MB to about 494 MB. Several OS releases in the field. People run Bullseye, Bookworm and Trixie, 32-bit and 64-bit. The original project's own images were built on 2019's Raspbian Stretch. A thing on the wall. It has to survive network outages, power cuts and an HDMI cable getting bumped, with nobody at a keyboard. Existing behavior stays put. The first Immich commit landed on a Friday. By Monday the fork existed and a pull request offering the work upstream was open. That gate stayed in force through every release after it. The image. A fork of pi-gen builds a headless Lite image: flash it, put your wifi details in wifi-config.txt on the boot partition, and the frame comes up with no SSH. Before rc1, a Pi Zero W driving a Toshiba laptop panel at 1366x768 through an HDMI-to-LVDS board booted that image, joined wifi from the file, and ran an Immich slideshow with HEIC photos without running out of memory. CI builds the same image under QEMU in about 48 minutes. Every photoframe tag now needs a matching pi-gen tag. rc1, April 18. Tested on a Pi 3B+ with Immich. The same week the Python 3 work went upstream again as a 30-commit pull request, which is still open. rc2, October 1, and the next eight hours. rc2 went out a little after midnight Eastern. By that morning, QA on a Pi 4 flashed with an image built from the rc2 commit had filed three bugs, and a second 32-bit board confirmed all three: The image's web UI had no login. pi-gen put the credentials file under /boot/firmware ; photoframe looked in /boot . The fix installs everything from apt, tested in an emulated Bullseye and on a Pi 5 running Trixie. Forcing pip with --break-system-packages was ruled out. One failed album refresh marked the album empty and blanked the frame for up to an hour. On a 464-photo album, an outage under fifteen minutes was enough. Now the frame keeps its photos, retries every minute, and refetched 25 seconds after the network came back in testing. Rotation and overscan settings never reached config.txt , because the path had been relative since the Python 3 port. Fixing it led to the question of power loss mid-write. An fsck of the boot partition two seconds after a write found config.txt truncated to zero bytes. One more fsync fixed it, then 40 concurrent changes and 50 rounds of parallel writes came back clean. The rc2 remediation pull request went through four independent review passes plus a Pi 4 boot on the fake-KMS driver. Each pass was answered with a commit. I made the scope calls: tvservice is deprecated but its code path stays where the command exists, and updater bugs move to 3.1. October 6: 3.0.0. rc2 was recut on October 5 with the remediation merged. v3.0.0 was tagged the next day at the same commit. Between the last release candidate and the stable release, nothing changed but the image builder's branch and the release notes. The stable release is the candidate that survived. A Browse button lists your albums, names match without regard to case, and the service retries with backoff when the server is unreachable. Displays without tvservice . The display size comes from the framebuffer, with health checks at startup. Home automation. /control/screenon and /control/screenoff over HTTP. Power-safe settings. config.txt edits survive a power cut and keep rotation and overscan lines across driver changes. Clean logs. Credentials no longer reach the log, and the log now carries normal messages. What I would do differently Start with the hardware gate. It arrived in April because an agent shipped a release nobody had run; it belonged in the September roadmap next to the route rule. And write the final-release order into RELEASE.md before cutting the first final release. On release day the 3.0.0 branch was made before master was fast-forwarded. It came out right, but the order lived in a session, not in the doc. Links Repo: https://github.com/dev-brewery/photoframe v3.0.0 release and SD card image: https://github.com/dev-brewery/photoframe/releases/tag/v3.0.0 Image builder: https://github.com/dev-brewery/pi-gen Earlier post: The Photo Frame I Didn't Have Time to Fix Why a rule like the hardware gate has to be a mechanism: Prompts Are Requests. Hooks Are Law.
items.summary_html:
Thirteen months from forking an abandoned Raspberry Pi project to its first stable release, and why the release only counted once a real Pi had run it.

Summary

photoframe is Henric Andersson's Raspberry Pi project that shows random photos from Google Photos like a picture frame. In 2025 Google cut the Photos Library API down to photos an app uploaded itself, and the frame had nothing left to read. I self-host Immich, so I forked the project in September 2025 to teach it Immich.

On October 6, 2026, the fork shipped v3.0.0, its first stable release: Python 3, Immich as the main photo source, display handling for current Raspberry Pi OS, and a flashable SD card image. Against the original project's master that is 65 files, 4,686 lines added and 1,662 removed, across 43 merged pull requests.

The code was written with AI agents. The release discipline was not optional, and it came from one bad morning in April: nothing gets pushed, tagged, released, or sent upstream until it has run on Pi hardware. The worst bugs in this write-up were caught by that rule.

I covered the early part in The Photo Frame I Didn't Have Time to Fix. This is the whole arc, through 3.0.0.

The problem

Three things were true at once:

  1. The photo source was gone. Google's API change left the frame with an empty library. Immich, which already held my photos, had no support.
  2. The base was stuck in the past. Upstream had a Python 3 branch whose own commit message read "Major update to python 3, still many things left to test." It never reached master. And Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm dropped tvservice, the tool photoframe used to find out what display it was plugged into.
  3. I didn't have the time. A port, a new service, an installer, an image, and testing across Pi models and screens is a second job. Without agents it doesn't happen at all.
Constraints
  • Small, old hardware. A Pi Zero W has 512 MB of memory. Full-size phone photos froze a Pi 3B+ until the frame learned to ask Immich for a preview first. Peak memory on an 800x480 panel went from about 1,061 MB to about 494 MB.
  • Several OS releases in the field. People run Bullseye, Bookworm and Trixie, 32-bit and 64-bit. The original project's own images were built on 2019's Raspbian Stretch.
  • A thing on the wall. It has to survive network outages, power cuts and an HDMI cable getting bumped, with nobody at a keyboard.
  • Existing behavior stays put. The first rule in the project's CLAUDE.md, in capitals: "NEVER modify existing routes for Immich features." Immich got its own /immichconfig route.
How the work ran

September 2025. The first Immich commit landed on a Friday. By Monday the fork existed and a pull request offering the work upstream was open. The agents ran as roles: an architect wrote phased roadmaps, I approved them as the product manager, a developer built, and a QA agent tested. When the developer agent added handlers to server.py anyway, the next commit was titled "Revert unauthorized changes."

April 2026: the morning it went too far. I came back for a real release push. On April 11, inside about eight minutes, an automated session rebased the Python 3 branch onto master, pushed master, created a v3.0.0 tag and release, created a dev branch, forked the Raspberry Pi image builder, and closed my upstream pull request by deleting the branch behind it. None of it had run on a Pi.

The answer was a written rollout plan with an eight-row damage assessment and one gate:

Nothing gets pushed, tagged, released, or sent upstream until it's been tested on Pi hardware.

That gate stayed in force through every release after it.

The image. A fork of pi-gen builds a headless Lite image: flash it, put your wifi details in wifi-config.txt on the boot partition, and the frame comes up with no SSH. Before rc1, a Pi Zero W driving a Toshiba laptop panel at 1366x768 through an HDMI-to-LVDS board booted that image, joined wifi from the file, and ran an Immich slideshow with HEIC photos without running out of memory. CI builds the same image under QEMU in about 48 minutes. Every photoframe tag now needs a matching pi-gen tag.

rc1, April 18. Tested on a Pi 3B+ with Immich. The same week the Python 3 work went upstream again as a 30-commit pull request, which is still open.

rc2, October 1, and the next eight hours. rc2 went out a little after midnight Eastern. By that morning, QA on a Pi 4 flashed with an image built from the rc2 commit had filed three bugs, and a second 32-bit board confirmed all three:

  • The image's web UI had no login. pi-gen put the credentials file under /boot/firmware; photoframe looked in /boot. The rc1 and rc2 images both shipped an open settings page.
  • The shutdown button did nothing on Bookworm. The kernel's GPIO numbering now starts at 512, so pin 3 is 515. That code dated from 2018.
  • Normal log messages never reached the log. Which also hid a worse bug, found by reading the code: the Immich API key and the Google OAuth token were being written to the log. The fixes went in with the credential change first, so the log never ran at INFO level while it still recorded keys.

All three were fixed and re-verified on the Pi 4 the same afternoon.

October 2 to 5: QA and review until it was boring. From rc2 to release, thirty issues and thirteen pull requests were opened. A few that stand out:

  • install.sh died at its pip step on Bookworm. The fix installs everything from apt, tested in an emulated Bullseye and on a Pi 5 running Trixie. Forcing pip with --break-system-packages was ruled out.
  • One failed album refresh marked the album empty and blanked the frame for up to an hour. On a 464-photo album, an outage under fifteen minutes was enough. Now the frame keeps its photos, retries every minute, and refetched 25 seconds after the network came back in testing.
  • Rotation and overscan settings never reached config.txt, because the path had been relative since the Python 3 port. Fixing it led to the question of power loss mid-write. An fsck of the boot partition two seconds after a write found config.txt truncated to zero bytes. One more fsync fixed it, then 40 concurrent changes and 50 rounds of parallel writes came back clean.
  • The rc2 remediation pull request went through four independent review passes plus a Pi 4 boot on the fake-KMS driver. Each pass was answered with a commit.

I made the scope calls: tvservice is deprecated but its code path stays where the command exists, and updater bugs move to 3.1.

October 6: 3.0.0. rc2 was recut on October 5 with the remediation merged. v3.0.0 was tagged the next day at the same commit. Between the last release candidate and the stable release, nothing changed but the image builder's branch and the release notes. The stable release is the candidate that survived.

What shipped
  • Immich, sized for the hardware. Preview images by default, full size only when /proc/meminfo and ImageMagick's limits allow it. HEIC works. A Browse button lists your albums, names match without regard to case, and the service retries with backoff when the server is unreachable.
  • Displays without tvservice. The display size comes from the framebuffer, with health checks at startup.
  • Home automation. /control/screenon and /control/screenoff over HTTP.
  • Power-safe settings. config.txt edits survive a power cut and keep rotation and overscan lines across driver changes.
  • Clean logs. Credentials no longer reach the log, and the log now carries normal messages.
  • An SD card image (Bookworm Lite, 854 MB zipped) and a migration script that moves an existing install from the original project to the 3.0.0 release branch, installs from apt only, and stops on anything older than Bullseye.
Outcome
Measure Result Fork to first stable release Sept 8, 2025 to Oct 6, 2026 Change against the original master 65 files, +4,686 / -1,662 lines Merged pull requests at release 43 Issues and PRs opened between rc2 and 3.0.0 30 and 13 Bugs from the first Pi 4 rc2 test, found to fixed and re-verified about 2 hours, same day Peak memory, Pi 3B+ at 800x480 about 1,061 MB down to about 494 MB Supported OS Bullseye, Bookworm, Trixie; 32 and 64 bit Supported Immich v2.x (v3 planned for 3.1)

The release notes list six known issues, all planned for 3.1. Two of them, rotation ignored under the KMS display driver and a cropped picture after an HDMI replug, were found on hardware and documented, with a workaround where one exists, instead of being guessed at.

What I would do differently

Start with the hardware gate. It arrived in April because an agent shipped a release nobody had run; it belonged in the September roadmap next to the route rule. And write the final-release order into RELEASE.md before cutting the first final release. On release day the 3.0.0 branch was made before master was fast-forwarded. It came out right, but the order lived in a session, not in the doc.

Links
  • Repo: https://github.com/dev-brewery/photoframe
  • v3.0.0 release and SD card image: https://github.com/dev-brewery/photoframe/releases/tag/v3.0.0
  • Image builder: https://github.com/dev-brewery/pi-gen
  • Earlier post: The Photo Frame I Didn't Have Time to Fix
  • Why a rule like the hardware gate has to be a mechanism: Prompts Are Requests. Hooks Are Law.

items.title: Hyperagent Review 2026: What \"Agents That Ship Real Work\" Actually Delivers
items.summary: Hyperagent promises a fleet of AI agents that research, build and keep deliverables alive inside Slack, your inbox or a schedule. I went through the product, the docs, the billing model and the published example runs to work out who it is for, what a job really costs, and where the rough edges are. If you have been anywhere near the AI-agent conversation this year, you have probably seen Hyperagent’s tagline: “Agents that ship real, powerful work.” It is a bold line in a category full of chatbots that answer a question and forget you. So I spent a few evenings with Hyperagent — the marketing site, the four-lesson onboarding path, the billing docs and the example jobs it shows on its homepage — to figure out whether Hyperagent is a genuinely different kind of tool or just another agent wrapper with a nicer landing page. Because a lot of what Hyperagent produces ends up as a website, a landing page or a small app, I also kept a prompt-to-product builder, Begin , open in the next tab as a point of comparison for that specific slice of the workflow — more on how the two fit together at the end. Hyperagent leads with finished deliverables — a hiring dashboard, a brand transformation, an out-of-home campaign — and prints the minutes and dollars each one took. What Hyperagent is, in one loop Hyperagent’s own docs describe the whole product as a single loop: you ask, the agent works, you get the finished thing, and it remembers. That last clause is the differentiator Hyperagent keeps coming back to. Its agents are not stateless chat sessions; they are configured teammates with a name, instructions, tools and knowledge, and they propose new memories and skills from real runs that you then approve or reject. Three words show up everywhere in Hyperagent: A thread holds one piece of work — the conversation, the tools that ran, and every artifact produced. An agent is a teammate you configure once. The same Hyperagent agent appears in a thread, in Slack, or on a Monday-morning schedule. Learning is how a Hyperagent agent gets better: it proposes memories and skills from runs, and you decide what sticks. That model is closer to “hire a junior and train them” than to “prompt a model”, and it shapes everything else about how Hyperagent feels. Who Hyperagent is for Hyperagent is aimed at teams that want output, not answers. The example jobs on the homepage are telling: a cinematic real-estate marketing package from a listing, a hiring command center that sources and ranks candidates with skill sliders, a complete brand identity with packaging and a launch site, and an out-of-home campaign with billboard research and mock-ups. None of those is a “write me a paragraph” task. They are multi-step projects that Hyperagent runs in its own computing environment with real browsers, real shells and access to whatever you would hand a new hire. If your work is mostly conversational — drafting emails, summarising documents — Hyperagent is overkill. If your work is “go research this, build the thing, and keep it updated when the world changes”, Hyperagent is squarely pointed at you. Getting started: four lessons, one hour Hyperagent’s onboarding is unusually well thought out. The “Start here” path is four short lessons that chain into each other: Your first thread — do real work in five minutes with nothing configured. Your first agent — turn a job worth repeating into a named teammate. Teach it something — save your first memory and watch Hyperagent learn. Put it where you work — move the agent into Slack, a schedule, or your inbox. Hyperagent says the whole path takes about an hour, and reading through it that estimate looks honest. The docs also include a wizard for migrating an existing OpenClaw agent, which tells you something about who Hyperagent expects to be switching over. The onboarding is four lessons — thread, agent, memory, surface — and Hyperagent’s docs are refreshingly free of fluff. Where Hyperagent runs: Slack, Telegram, webhooks, schedules One of the more practical decisions Hyperagent has made is to treat the chat window as just one surface. You can @-mention a Hyperagent agent in Slack, connect it to Telegram, trigger it from a webhook, or run it on a schedule. Deliverables go to Slack, your inbox, “anywhere”, and Hyperagent keeps them current as inputs change — the “work never goes stale” promise. For a team already living in Slack this is the difference between a tool people try once and a tool that becomes part of the weekly rhythm. It is also where Hyperagent’s fleet framing makes sense: you deploy, connect and manage agents from one command center rather than one browser tab each. What Hyperagent can produce Hyperagent lists websites, video, slides, documents and dashboards as first-class outputs, and it is specific about the websites: HTML that renders live, “built and hosted, not pasted into a doc”. The homepage examples cover market-signal briefs, candidate slates, comp analyses and landing pages. Every search, decision and artifact is visible as it is built, which matters when you are trying to trust an agent with a multi-hour job. Hyperagent pricing: dollar credits, not tokens This is the part I spent the most time on, because Hyperagent’s billing changed in August 2026 and the docs are candid about it. Hyperagent bills through credits denominated in dollars . You choose a monthly plan, pay its price at the start of each billing period, and that money comes back as credit plus a bonus that grows with your plan. Usage spends the balance down. Pay As You Go and annual plans are no longer offered as of August 2026, and the early-user bonus subsidy was replaced by a progressive bonus. Shared billing lets multiple members bill to one organisation payment method. Usage can be tracked at the account, agent or thread level, and invoices are downloadable. Hyperagent also documents connecting a ChatGPT subscription as an option. The most useful pricing data is on the homepage itself, where Hyperagent prints the real cost of its example runs: Out-of-home campaign research and visuals: 8 minutes, $6.41 Cinematic real-estate video package: 29 minutes, $24.79 Hiring command center with ranked candidates: 22 minutes, $14.18 Complete brand transformation with launch site: 15 minutes, $3.88 Those are single-digit to low-double-digit dollar amounts for jobs that would take a contractor a day. The catch is variance: Hyperagent’s docs push you to “choose the right model for each job”, which is a polite way of saying the same brief can cost very different amounts depending on the model an agent reaches for. Hyperagent’s billing section covers credits, plans, shared billing, usage and invoices — and states plainly that Pay As You Go and annual plans were dropped in August 2026. What Hyperagent gets right Deliverables, not chat. Hyperagent optimises for finished artifacts that live somewhere useful. Memory that you control. Agents propose memories and skills; a human approves them. That is the right default. Multi-surface by design. Slack, Telegram, webhooks and schedules are core, not add-ons. Transparent cost per job. Printing “$6.41, 8 minutes” on the homepage is a level of honesty most agent platforms avoid. Serious onboarding. The lesson path and knowledge base are better than most products twice Hyperagent’s age. Where Hyperagent falls short No pay-as-you-go anymore. If you only need Hyperagent for a project a quarter, a monthly plan is a poor fit. Cost variance. Dollar credits are clear, but per-run cost depends on model choice, and Hyperagent’s own docs devote a page to controlling it. The name is crowded. Searching “hyperagent” also surfaces Hyperbrowser’s open-source HyperAgent for Playwright, Meta’s “Hyperagents” self-improving-agent research, and an unrelated blockchain protocol. Make sure you are on hyperagent.com. Generalist output. Hyperagent’s landing pages and sites are competent, but a builder that specialises in shipping products still produces a stronger website from the same brief. Hyperagent vs the alternatives Against chat-first assistants, Hyperagent wins on persistence and deliverables. Against pure automation platforms, Hyperagent wins on judgment — its agents research and decide rather than execute a fixed flow. Where Hyperagent is weakest is the last mile of a specific artifact type: if what you need is a production website or a native app, a dedicated builder does that one job more thoroughly, which is exactly why I kept Begin open alongside it. Verdict: is Hyperagent worth it in 2026? Yes, for teams with recurring multi-step work that ends in a real deliverable and a Slack channel to receive it. Hyperagent’s loop — ask, work, deliver, remember — is coherent, the billing is honest, and the published per-job costs are low enough to justify a monthly plan quickly. It is a weaker fit for occasional users now that pay-as-you-go is gone, and for anyone whose real need is a single polished product rather than a stream of briefs. You can walk through Hyperagent’s first thread yourself before deciding. The alternative worth keeping next to it: Begin Two things about Hyperagent pushed me to keep a specialist builder open: the loss of a pay-as-you-go option, and the fact that its websites and apps are one output among many rather than the whole point. Begin is the one I used. Five free credits, no card — exactly one real first build, so you can paste a domain and judge the output before paying anything. Prompt or paste a domain — Begin fetches the source, reads the design tokens, rewrites the copy and produces a site you own, or builds an iOS app, Android app or Chrome extension from the same brief. Predictable credits — every plan includes 100 credits a month; a first build costs 5 and every change after that costs 1, with unused credits rolling over on paid plans and failed builds refunded automatically. Shipping is built in — hosting on Begin’s edge with TLS and your own domain, sign-in, database, storage and Stripe payments wired into each project. From $49 a month , with a $99 team tier for shared workspaces and a brand kit. If the job is “research it, build it, keep it current in Slack”, stay with Hyperagent. If the job is “turn this brief into a product I can put in front of customers”, spend five minutes on Begin first. Photo by David Levêque on Unsplash
items.summary_html:
Hyperagent promises a fleet of AI agents that research, build and keep deliverables alive inside Slack, your inbox or a schedule. I went through the product, the docs, the billing model and the published example runs to work out who it is for, what a job really costs, and where the rough edges are.

If you have been anywhere near the AI-agent conversation this year, you have probably seen Hyperagent’s tagline: “Agents that ship real, powerful work.” It is a bold line in a category full of chatbots that answer a question and forget you. So I spent a few evenings with Hyperagent — the marketing site, the four-lesson onboarding path, the billing docs and the example jobs it shows on its homepage — to figure out whether Hyperagent is a genuinely different kind of tool or just another agent wrapper with a nicer landing page.

Because a lot of what Hyperagent produces ends up as a website, a landing page or a small app, I also kept a prompt-to-product builder, Begin, open in the next tab as a point of comparison for that specific slice of the workflow — more on how the two fit together at the end.

Hyperagent leads with finished deliverables — a hiring dashboard, a brand transformation, an out-of-home campaign — and prints the minutes and dollars each one took.

What Hyperagent is, in one loop

Hyperagent’s own docs describe the whole product as a single loop: you ask, the agent works, you get the finished thing, and it remembers. That last clause is the differentiator Hyperagent keeps coming back to. Its agents are not stateless chat sessions; they are configured teammates with a name, instructions, tools and knowledge, and they propose new memories and skills from real runs that you then approve or reject.

Three words show up everywhere in Hyperagent:

  • A thread holds one piece of work — the conversation, the tools that ran, and every artifact produced.
  • An agent is a teammate you configure once. The same Hyperagent agent appears in a thread, in Slack, or on a Monday-morning schedule.
  • Learning is how a Hyperagent agent gets better: it proposes memories and skills from runs, and you decide what sticks.

That model is closer to “hire a junior and train them” than to “prompt a model”, and it shapes everything else about how Hyperagent feels.

Who Hyperagent is for

Hyperagent is aimed at teams that want output, not answers. The example jobs on the homepage are telling: a cinematic real-estate marketing package from a listing, a hiring command center that sources and ranks candidates with skill sliders, a complete brand identity with packaging and a launch site, and an out-of-home campaign with billboard research and mock-ups. None of those is a “write me a paragraph” task. They are multi-step projects that Hyperagent runs in its own computing environment with real browsers, real shells and access to whatever you would hand a new hire.

If your work is mostly conversational — drafting emails, summarising documents — Hyperagent is overkill. If your work is “go research this, build the thing, and keep it updated when the world changes”, Hyperagent is squarely pointed at you.

Getting started: four lessons, one hour

Hyperagent’s onboarding is unusually well thought out. The “Start here” path is four short lessons that chain into each other:

  1. Your first thread — do real work in five minutes with nothing configured.
  2. Your first agent — turn a job worth repeating into a named teammate.
  3. Teach it something — save your first memory and watch Hyperagent learn.
  4. Put it where you work — move the agent into Slack, a schedule, or your inbox.

Hyperagent says the whole path takes about an hour, and reading through it that estimate looks honest. The docs also include a wizard for migrating an existing OpenClaw agent, which tells you something about who Hyperagent expects to be switching over.

The onboarding is four lessons — thread, agent, memory, surface — and Hyperagent’s docs are refreshingly free of fluff.

Where Hyperagent runs: Slack, Telegram, webhooks, schedules

One of the more practical decisions Hyperagent has made is to treat the chat window as just one surface. You can @-mention a Hyperagent agent in Slack, connect it to Telegram, trigger it from a webhook, or run it on a schedule. Deliverables go to Slack, your inbox, “anywhere”, and Hyperagent keeps them current as inputs change — the “work never goes stale” promise.

For a team already living in Slack this is the difference between a tool people try once and a tool that becomes part of the weekly rhythm. It is also where Hyperagent’s fleet framing makes sense: you deploy, connect and manage agents from one command center rather than one browser tab each.

What Hyperagent can produce

Hyperagent lists websites, video, slides, documents and dashboards as first-class outputs, and it is specific about the websites: HTML that renders live, “built and hosted, not pasted into a doc”. The homepage examples cover market-signal briefs, candidate slates, comp analyses and landing pages. Every search, decision and artifact is visible as it is built, which matters when you are trying to trust an agent with a multi-hour job.

Hyperagent pricing: dollar credits, not tokens

This is the part I spent the most time on, because Hyperagent’s billing changed in August 2026 and the docs are candid about it.

  • Hyperagent bills through credits denominated in dollars. You choose a monthly plan, pay its price at the start of each billing period, and that money comes back as credit plus a bonus that grows with your plan. Usage spends the balance down.
  • Pay As You Go and annual plans are no longer offered as of August 2026, and the early-user bonus subsidy was replaced by a progressive bonus.
  • Shared billing lets multiple members bill to one organisation payment method.
  • Usage can be tracked at the account, agent or thread level, and invoices are downloadable.
  • Hyperagent also documents connecting a ChatGPT subscription as an option.

The most useful pricing data is on the homepage itself, where Hyperagent prints the real cost of its example runs:

  • Out-of-home campaign research and visuals: 8 minutes, $6.41
  • Cinematic real-estate video package: 29 minutes, $24.79
  • Hiring command center with ranked candidates: 22 minutes, $14.18
  • Complete brand transformation with launch site: 15 minutes, $3.88

Those are single-digit to low-double-digit dollar amounts for jobs that would take a contractor a day. The catch is variance: Hyperagent’s docs push you to “choose the right model for each job”, which is a polite way of saying the same brief can cost very different amounts depending on the model an agent reaches for.

Hyperagent’s billing section covers credits, plans, shared billing, usage and invoices — and states plainly that Pay As You Go and annual plans were dropped in August 2026.

What Hyperagent gets right
  • Deliverables, not chat. Hyperagent optimises for finished artifacts that live somewhere useful.
  • Memory that you control. Agents propose memories and skills; a human approves them. That is the right default.
  • Multi-surface by design. Slack, Telegram, webhooks and schedules are core, not add-ons.
  • Transparent cost per job. Printing “$6.41, 8 minutes” on the homepage is a level of honesty most agent platforms avoid.
  • Serious onboarding. The lesson path and knowledge base are better than most products twice Hyperagent’s age.
Where Hyperagent falls short
  • No pay-as-you-go anymore. If you only need Hyperagent for a project a quarter, a monthly plan is a poor fit.
  • Cost variance. Dollar credits are clear, but per-run cost depends on model choice, and Hyperagent’s own docs devote a page to controlling it.
  • The name is crowded. Searching “hyperagent” also surfaces Hyperbrowser’s open-source HyperAgent for Playwright, Meta’s “Hyperagents” self-improving-agent research, and an unrelated blockchain protocol. Make sure you are on hyperagent.com.
  • Generalist output. Hyperagent’s landing pages and sites are competent, but a builder that specialises in shipping products still produces a stronger website from the same brief.
Hyperagent vs the alternatives

Against chat-first assistants, Hyperagent wins on persistence and deliverables. Against pure automation platforms, Hyperagent wins on judgment — its agents research and decide rather than execute a fixed flow. Where Hyperagent is weakest is the last mile of a specific artifact type: if what you need is a production website or a native app, a dedicated builder does that one job more thoroughly, which is exactly why I kept Begin open alongside it.

Verdict: is Hyperagent worth it in 2026?

Yes, for teams with recurring multi-step work that ends in a real deliverable and a Slack channel to receive it. Hyperagent’s loop — ask, work, deliver, remember — is coherent, the billing is honest, and the published per-job costs are low enough to justify a monthly plan quickly. It is a weaker fit for occasional users now that pay-as-you-go is gone, and for anyone whose real need is a single polished product rather than a stream of briefs. You can walk through Hyperagent’s first thread yourself before deciding.

The alternative worth keeping next to it: Begin

Two things about Hyperagent pushed me to keep a specialist builder open: the loss of a pay-as-you-go option, and the fact that its websites and apps are one output among many rather than the whole point. Begin is the one I used.

  • Five free credits, no card — exactly one real first build, so you can paste a domain and judge the output before paying anything.
  • Prompt or paste a domain — Begin fetches the source, reads the design tokens, rewrites the copy and produces a site you own, or builds an iOS app, Android app or Chrome extension from the same brief.
  • Predictable credits — every plan includes 100 credits a month; a first build costs 5 and every change after that costs 1, with unused credits rolling over on paid plans and failed builds refunded automatically.
  • Shipping is built in — hosting on Begin’s edge with TLS and your own domain, sign-in, database, storage and Stripe payments wired into each project.
  • From $49 a month, with a $99 team tier for shared workspaces and a brand kit.

If the job is “research it, build it, keep it current in Slack”, stay with Hyperagent. If the job is “turn this brief into a product I can put in front of customers”, spend five minutes on Begin first.
