items.title: Neural Petri flows for chemical reactions
items.summary: Petri nets have been used to describe chemical processes such as reactions.They map well to chemistry: Places are the bonds between atoms and the free valence of each atom, a token is a unit of bond order, a transition forms or breaks a bond, the conserved quantities are the valence budgets of the atoms, and the enabling rule is the valence rule. These semantics are not guaranteed by learned models of reactions or neural networks that are built on Petri nets that use the net as a scaffold for message passing. Here, we ask what architecture remains a Petri net for every value of its weights. We find the answer in the theory, where all semantics of a net share the firing form $m^\prime=m+C\sigma$, locality, as enabling reads only the inputs of a transition, and the enabling rule, and we prove that conservation forces the firing form and that non-negativity forces the enabling rule on local rate laws. This leaves free the rate law, which is the propensity of each transition to fire. We introduce Neural Petri Flow, which learns this rate law, or a readout for classification, and hard-wires the rest as parameter-free layers. On what we denote a valence net, atom mapping, reaction classification, and forward prediction become three tasks on one firing vector. Without training, the minimum firing vector maps 88.8% of the curated Golden set against 85.6% for RXNMapper, and 88.7 against 77.9% of the enzymatic reactions of EnzymeMap. On USPTO-480K, NPF trained on these firing vectors predicts 87.7% of the products and 67.4% when trained on a 1% subset of the training reactions. EC numbers of ECREACT are predicted at the third level for 90.2% of reactions, 5.6 points ahead of the best published method. With electrons as tokens, the same token game predicts 90.5% of the elementary steps of FlowER first, ahead of the published baseline, and every top-1 prediction is a valid molecule without a filter.

items.title: Conformal Prediction Sets Quantify Information Gain: A Theoretical Perspective
items.summary: Conformal prediction is a popular tool for uncertainty quantification that outputs prediction sets with finite-sample coverage guarantees. While prediction set size is commonly used as a heuristic measure of uncertainty, the information-theoretic basis for this interpretation remains poorly understood. In this work, we provide such a foundation using a decision-theoretic generalization of entropy tailored to set-valued prediction. In particular, we introduce a family of generalized information measures based on the size and coverage of conformal prediction sets. Notably, Shannon mutual information admits an exact integral representation in terms of these measures. We then show that, in standard classification settings, the reduction in conformal set size from additional information (i) is sandwiched between calibration-dependent members of this family and (ii) obeys a data processing inequality, both up to finite-sample calibration and model error terms. Together, our results formally relate conformal prediction to classical information-theoretic quantities and justify using set-size reduction as an information gain metric. Empirically, we validate our theory across 11 classification settings and show that set-size reduction and Shannon mutual information can rank features differently in a greedy feature selection experiment.

items.title: The Chunking Dilemma: Why RAG Fails Before Retrieval Even Starts
items.summary_html:
Part 4 of the Production RAG Series — Demystifying the Ingestion Pipeline, The Goldilocks Problem of Chunk Size, and Baseline Splitting Strategies.

Hey friends! Welcome back to our ongoing series on building real-world, production-grade Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

In Part 3, we had an honest conversation about the “infinite context window” myth. We saw why simply giving an LLM hundreds of pages of company documentation isn’t the magical solution it sounds like:

  • It drastically increases API costs.
  • It drives up query latency.
  • It dilutes the model’s attention.
  • When too much information is placed into the prompt, models struggle with the “Lost in the Middle” phenomenon — missing facts buried among irrelevant content.

So we arrived at a much more practical conclusion:

Don’t give the LLM everything. Give it only the specific information it actually needs.

Sounds simple, right?

Well… this is where things get interesting. Because before we can retrieve the right information, we first have to decide: what exactly are we retrieving?

A 500-page employee handbook isn’t stored as one giant text block. We have to break it down into smaller pieces. Those pieces are called chunks. And suddenly, a seemingly simple question appears: Where exactly should we cut the document?

Cut in the wrong place, and you destroy the exact context you were trying to preserve. Cut too large, and your search becomes blurry and imprecise.

That is the Chunking Dilemma.

A Quick Road Ahead:
A full production RAG pipeline consists of:
Documents → Chunking → Embeddings → Vector / Document DB → Retrieval → LLM Prompt
If terms like “embeddings” or “vector databases” sound new, don’t worry! We have dedicated deep-dive articles coming up for each of those topics. In fact, because chunking is so foundational, we are splitting it into two digestible reads:
Today (Part 4): The Ingestion Pipeline, the Goldilocks chunk-sizing problem, and baseline splitting strategies.
Part 5: Advanced chunking architectures (Bounded Semantic Chunking, Parent-Document Retrieval, Breadcrumbs, and Anthropic’s Contextual Retrieval).
Let’s dive in!
Before Retrieval, There Is an Entire Pipeline

Let’s zoom out for a moment. A production RAG system is split into two fundamentally different journeys:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        OFFLINE INGESTION PIPELINE                      │
│                                                                        │
│   Raw Sources (PDFs, Wikis, Codebases, Confluence, DBs, Tickets)       │
│                                  │                                     │
│                                  ▼                                     │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │ Parse & Clean: Extract text, tables, code, headers             │   │
│   └──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                  ▼                                     │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │ CHUNKING: Break documents into meaningful, retrievable units   │   │
│   └──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                  ▼                                     │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │ Metadata Enrichment: Breadcrumbs, page, source, parent_id...   │   │
│   └──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                  ▼                                     │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │ Embedding Generation: Text → Vector coordinates                │   │
│   └──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                  ▼                                     │
│   Vector Database & Document Store (Indexed for Search)                │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Notice something critical: Chunking isn’t a minor preprocessing detail. It defines the physical units of memory your search engine will later evaluate.

Now compare that with what happens when a user asks a question:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         ONLINE QUERY PIPELINE                          │
│                                                                        │
│   User Question                                                        │
│         │                                                              │
│         ▼                                                              │
│   Query Embedding                                                      │
│         │                                                              │
│         ▼                                                              │
│   Vector Search / Keyword Retrieval                                    │
│         │                                                              │
│         ▼                                                              │
│   Top-K Matching Chunks Retrieved                                      │
│         │                                                              │
│         ▼                                                              │
│   Reranking & Metadata Filtering                                       │
│         │                                                              │
│         ▼                                                              │
│   LLM Prompt + Retrieved Context                                       │
│         │                                                              │
│         ▼                                                              │
│   Accurate Answer                                                      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The online query pipeline gets all the attention because it touches the user interface. But the offline ingestion pipeline quietly sets the hard ceiling on what your system is capable of finding. And this is where our story begins.

Storytime: The Day the Staging Bot Lied

Imagine you’re building your first enterprise RAG prototype. You follow a quickstart tutorial, load a few sample PDFs, and write those famous three lines of code:

# The tutorial dream
text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=1000, 
    chunk_overlap=200
)
chunks = text_splitter.split_documents(docs)

You test it with five sample questions. Five out of five answers look brilliant! High fives all around. You demo it to your team, everyone is impressed, and you connect the bot to your company’s actual knowledge base: 50,000 files spanning employee policies, SEC financial filings, API documentation, and architecture wikis.

Two days later, Slack starts blowing up:

  • “The bot says our Q3 revenue dropped by 24%!” (Yet the official earnings release says global revenue grew by 24%).
  • “The bot told an employee they’re not eligible for parental leave!”
  • “The API endpoint the bot gave me doesn’t exist!”

Your first instinct is to blame the LLM. You assume the model is hallucinating, so you upgrade from GPT-4o-mini to Claude 3.5 Sonnet, lower the temperature to 0.0, and spend four hours rewriting the system prompt. Nothing fixes it.

Eventually, you stop looking at the LLM. You open your database and inspect the exact chunk that was retrieved for that financial query:

"...decreased by 24% due to unexpected supply chain disruptions in the European sector."

It looks like a reasonable sentence. Except it isn’t.

The chunk started right in the middle of a sentence! The text immediately preceding it had said:

“While overall global revenue grew by 24%, regional European shipping volume decreased by 24%…”

The retrieval system didn’t retrieve a complete thought. It retrieved a severed fragment of a thought. And the LLM had no choice but to answer using that mutilated fragment.

Here is the vital takeaway:

A retrieval system can only retrieve the pieces you created during ingestion. If those pieces are poorly designed, no multi-billion-parameter LLM or reranker can magically reconstruct the truth.
The “Goldilocks Dilemma” of Chunk Sizing

So, what should your chunk size be? 100 tokens? 500? 1,000? 2,000?

There is no universal magic number. We face the classic Goldilocks Problem: chunks can be too small, or they can be too large.

┌───────────────────────────────┐     ┌───────────────────────────────┐
│       CHUNKS TOO SMALL        │     │       CHUNKS TOO LARGE        │
│       (e.g., 50 tokens)       │     │     (e.g., 2,000 tokens)      │
├───────────────────────────────┤     ├───────────────────────────────┤
│ ✗ Missing critical context    │     │ ✗ Multiple mixed topics       │
│ ✗ Severed rules & exceptions  │     │ ✗ Mean pooling dilution       │
│ ✗ The "Half-Truth" catalyst   │     │ ✗ Semantic blur in search     │
│ ✗ Orphaned pronouns           │     │ ✗ Wasted prompt token budget  │
└───────────────────────────────┘     └───────────────────────────────┘
1. The Small Chunk Trap (The “Half-Truth” Catalyst)

It’s tempting to think: “If I make my chunks tiny (like 1 or 2 sentences), search precision will be laser-sharp because the chunk will match the user’s exact keywords!”

While small chunks match search queries easily, they act as a direct catalyst for hallucinations and dangerous half-truths.

Consider this employee handbook policy:

“Employees are entitled to 20 days of paid vacation per year. However, contractors and interns are not eligible for paid vacation.”

If your chunker cuts too aggressively, it produces:

  • Chunk A: “Employees are entitled to 20 days of paid vacation per year.”
  • Chunk B: “However, contractors and interns are not eligible for paid vacation.”

Now an intern asks your company bot:
“Am I eligible for paid vacation?”

The retrieval system searches for “eligible paid vacation”. Chunk A looks like a 99% match. It retrieves Chunk A and sends it to the LLM.

The LLM reads: “Employees are entitled to 20 days of paid vacation per year.”
And what does it conclude?
“Yes! You are entitled to 20 days of paid vacation!”

Notice what happened here:

  • The LLM did not make up fake information from thin air.
  • What it said was technically written in the document.
  • But it produced a catastrophic half-truth because chunking separated the rule from its exception.

This happens whenever chunking splits:

  • A rule from its exception
  • A condition from its prerequisite
  • A definition from the term it defines
  • A pronoun (“it”, “they”) from its antecedent noun
Rule of Thumb: The goal of chunking is not “make every chunk exactly 400 tokens.” The goal is to create chunks that are independently meaningful units of thought.
2. The Large Chunk Trap (Semantic Blur & Mean Pooling Dilution)

So you might think: “If small chunks lose context, let’s make them huge! Say, 2,000 tokens. Modern embedding models can read thousands of tokens, so why not give it the whole section?”

Because you run into the opposite problem: Loss of Search Precision (Semantic Blur).

An embedding model does not store 2,000 separate concepts. It must compress that entire 2,000-token chunk into a single mathematical vector (e.g., 768 or 1,536 numbers).

Under the hood, most transformer embedding models do this through a mathematical operation called Mean Pooling: they calculate the mathematical average of all token vectors across the chunk!

Now imagine what that means in practice. Suppose a 2,000-token chunk covers four disparate topics:

  • Tokens 1–500: Office parking garage permits
  • Tokens 501–1000: Healthcare and dental coverage
  • Tokens 1001–1500: Kubernetes cluster access for engineers
  • Tokens 1501–2000: Client dinner expense policies and alcohol limits

When the embedding model computes the mean vector for this chunk, the vector’s direction in mathematical space is pulled in four completely different directions:

  • 25% Parking
  • 25% Health
  • 25% Kubernetes
  • 25% Dinner Expenses

Now, an employee asks:
“What is the maximum Food expense allowed for a client dinner?”

The user’s query is only 12 tokens. Its embedding vector is 100% focused on client dinners and expenses.

When your vector database calculates the Cosine Similarity between:

  • Query Vector (100% Dinner Expenses)
  • Giant Chunk Vector (25% Dinner Expenses + 25% Parking + 25% Health + 25% Kubernetes)

What happens? The similarity score drops significantly (e.g., to 0.48) because 75% of the giant chunk’s vector is pulling toward parking garages and server clusters!

Meanwhile, a focused 120-token chunk that only discussed client dinner expenses will score 0.89!

(Note: Those similarity numbers are illustrative, not universal laws. The key takeaway is the difference in semantic focus).

The information hasn’t disappeared from the 2,000-token chunk. But the representation used for retrieval has become an “averaged-out soup.” That is Semantic Blur.

The Chunking Sweet Spot

So we have two competing requirements:

  • Small chunks: High retrieval precision, but risk missing surrounding context.
  • Large chunks: Broad context, but risk semantic dilution and prompt bloat.

Instead of asking: “What is the best chunk size?”, the better engineering question is:

“What is the smallest unit of text that preserves enough self-contained meaning for my retrieval task?”

At this point, your natural instinct might be: “Okay, I get it. I shouldn’t make my chunks 50 tokens, and I shouldn’t make them 2,000 tokens. Let’s aim for that sweet spot! I’ll just open my Python script, configure chunk_size = 500, and start slicing.”

Hold on.

Before you write that line of code, there is a subtle, deceptive trap waiting for you.

The Silent Trap: Characters Are Not Tokens

When you configure chunk_size = 500 in a text splitter, ask yourself: 500 of what? In Python, length is measured in raw characters (letters, spaces, and punctuation):

text = "RAG pipeline"
len(text)  # Returns 12 characters

If you don’t supply a custom tokenizer, many standard splitters count 500 characters. In English prose, an average word is about 5 characters plus a space. That means a 500-character chunk is barely 80 to 100 words! Without realizing it, you just walked right back into the Small Chunk Trap.

And it gets more dangerous: embedding models and LLMs do not process characters or words. They process tokens.

While clean English prose follows a rough rule of thumb:

General English Rule of Thumb:
1 Token ≈ 0.75 words ≈ 4 characters

The real world is rarely that clean. Consider what happens when your enterprise document contains:

  • Indented Python or JavaScript code
  • Markdown tables with pipes, dashes, and whitespace
  • URLs, JSON payloads, and technical identifiers
  • Text in non-English languages (like Hindi, Japanese, or German)

In these scenarios, character-to-token ratios explode! A chunk that looks like an innocent 1,500 characters can easily expand into 700 tokens.

Why does this matter so much? Because of a number that trips up even experienced AI engineers: the embedding model’s context ceiling.

The 512-Token Truncation Trap

We often hear about frontier LLMs boasting massive 128k or 1-million-token context windows. But don’t confuse your Generation LLM with your Embedding Model:

  • Generation LLM Context Window (e.g., 128k for GPT-4o, 1M for Gemini): Determines how much total retrieved context you can feed to the prompt at query time.
  • Embedding Model Sequence Limit (e.g., 512 tokens for e5-base, bge-base, BERT): Determines how much text can be converted into a vector during the offline ingestion pipeline.

Many of the most popular, cost-effective open-source embedding models deployed across the industry have a hard sequence limit of just 512 tokens.

Now, picture what happens when that 1,500-character chunk (which expanded to 700 tokens) arrives at a 512-token embedding model:

The tokenizer silently applies truncation=True. It embeds the first 512 tokens, chops off the remaining 188 tokens, and tosses them in the trash!

There is no error thrown in your console. Your ingestion script happily prints 100% Ingested. Your vector database stores a vector. But the final 188 tokens never participated in the embedding. If the exact answer to your user's question lived in those truncated lines, your vector search will never find it.

Production Rule: Never design your chunking pipeline using raw character counts alone. Always measure and enforce chunk boundaries using the actual tokenizer and token limit of your target embedding model.

Now that we know we must measure in tokens and stay within our model’s physical limits, how do we actually slice the text?

Let’s explore the three foundational strategies.

Three Baseline Production Chunking Strategies

Now let’s look at the first three foundational chunking strategies used in real-world systems.

Strategy 1: Fixed-Size Chunking (The Naive Baseline)

This is the simplest approach: slice text every N characters or tokens unconditionally, like a cookie cutter.

Original sentence:
"Under clause 14, the total aggregate liability of the Vendor shall not exceed $1,000,000."
Fixed cut at character 60:
[Chunk 1]: "Under clause 14, the total aggregate liability of the Vendor"
[Chunk 2]: " shall not exceed $1,000,000."

If a user asks: “What is the vendor’s liability cap?”, vector search pulls Chunk 1 because it matches “liability of the Vendor”. But Chunk 1 has no numbers! The LLM reads Chunk 1 and answers: “The agreement mentions liability under clause 14, but does not state any dollar amount.”

Verdict: 🛑 Do not use this in production. It cuts words, severs numbers from clauses, and destroys grammar.

Strategy 2: Recursive Character Splitting (The Enterprise Workhorse)

For general unstructured text — articles, reports, memos, documentation — a recursive splitter is the standard baseline.

Instead of slicing text at an arbitrary position, it tries progressively more granular separators:

Paragraph (\n\n)  ──►  Line (\n)  ──►  Sentence (. )  ──►  Word ( )  ──►  Character ("")

It acts like a thoughtful editor. It first asks: “Can I keep entire paragraphs together within my chunk size limit?” If a paragraph is too long, it steps down and tries line breaks. If a line is still too long, it splits on sentences. It only ever splits words as an absolute last resort.

Raw Document
     │
     ├── Can this paragraph fit within chunk_size?
     │     ├── YES ──► Keep it together!
     │     └── NO  ──► Step down to line breaks (\n)
     │
     ├── Can this line fit?
     │     ├── YES ──► Keep it together!
     │     └── NO  ──► Step down to sentence endings (. )
     │
     └── Step down until pieces fit comfortably within token bounds.
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=400,        # Target tokens
    chunk_overlap=80,      # 20% safety net
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""]
)
Chunk Overlap: The Safety Net

Whenever you use recursive splitting, you should configure chunk overlap (typically 10% to 20% of your chunk size):

[ Chunk 1: Tokens 0 ──────────────► 400 ]
             [ Chunk 2: Tokens 320 ──────────────► 720 ]  (80-token overlap)
                          [ Chunk 3: Tokens 640 ──────────────► 1040 ]

Why overlap matters:
Sometimes, a critical clause spans across a chunk boundary:

Without Overlap:

  • Chunk 1: "...employees can claim reimbursement after..."
  • Chunk 2: "...submitting Form 104-B within 30 days."

The relationship between the requirement and the form is severed.

With Overlap:
The sliding window captures the complete boundary clause unbroken in Chunk 2!

The Trade-Off: More overlap means slightly more storage and duplicate text in your vector index. A starting point of 10%–20% (50 to 80 tokens = roughly 2–3 sentences) provides a solid safety margin.

Strategy 3: Structure-Aware Chunking (Markdown, Code, and Tables)

Humans don’t write in random blocks of 400 words. We write using explicit structures: headings, sections, code blocks, and tables.

When you run a naive text splitter on structured documents, you throw that structure away:

  • A sub-bullet point is separated from its parent # Heading.
  • A Python function gets cut across its loop body.
  • A table row is disconnected from its column headers.
1. Markdown Header Splitting

In technical manuals and wikis, headings (#, ##, ###) define logical units of thought.

Structure-aware splitters divide text based on these headings and automatically inject the heading path into each chunk’s metadata:

from langchain_text_splitters import MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter

headers_to_split_on = [
    ("#", "Section"),
    ("##", "Subsection"),
    ("###", "Topic")
]

markdown_splitter = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(
    headers_to_split_on=headers_to_split_on
)

Now, each chunk isn’t just floating text. It is an indexed object carrying its exact structural hierarchy in its metadata payload:

{
  "metadata": {
    "Section": "Benefits",
    "Subsection": "Health Insurance",
    "Topic": "Out-of-Network Coverage"
  },
  "page_content": "Employees can claim out-of-network reimbursement after..."
}

This structural metadata solves two major production problems:

  1. Prevents Orphan Text: Even if the chunk itself never mentions the words “Health Insurance”, the metadata permanently binds the text to its parent topic.
  2. Enables Metadata Filtering: At query time, you can pre-filter searches directly in your database (e.g., only search where "Section": "Benefits"), eliminating irrelevant company documents before vector search even begins!
2. Code-Aware Splitting

If you are indexing a software repository, chunking must respect the programming language’s Abstract Syntax Tree (AST):

def process_payment():
    try:
        charge_customer()
        update_order()
    except PaymentError:
        rollback()

Cutting this code block arbitrarily in the middle of the try block destroys its syntax and meaning. Language-aware splitters keep entire functions, classes, or imports together as single logical blocks.

3. The Table Problem (Financial 10-K & 10-Q Filings)

Tables are one of the fastest ways to break a naive RAG pipeline. Consider this balance sheet:

| Product Segment       | Q1 2024 ($M) | Q2 2024 ($M) | Q3 2024 ($M) |
| --------------------- | -----------: | -----------: | -----------: |
| Cloud Subscriptions   |       $4,200 |       $4,600 |       $5,100 |
| Professional Services |         $320 |         $310 |         $305 |

Now imagine a standard text splitter cuts this table horizontally when it hits a character limit:

  • Chunk 1:
    Product Segment | Q1 2024 | Q2 2024 | Q3 2024
    Cloud Subscriptions | $4,200 | $4,600 | $5,100
  • Chunk 2:
    Professional Services | $320 | $310 | $305

Now an analyst asks:
“What was Professional Services revenue in Q2 2024?”

The vector search retrieves Chunk 2. But Chunk 2 contains three bare numbers without the header Q2 2024! The retrieval succeeded, but answer generation fails because the structural context was lost.

The Production Fix for Tables:

  1. Use Table-Aware Parsers that convert rows into structured formats (like Markdown or JSON) that repeat the column headers on every slice:
{
  "Company": "ACME Corp",
  "Report": "Q3 2024",
  "Segment": "Professional Services",
  "Period": "Q2 2024",
  "Revenue": "$310M"
}

2. Now the number has complete meaning: Professional Services → Q2 2024 → Revenue → $310M.

Where Do We Go From Here?

We’ve now established the fundamentals:

  • The Ingestion Pipeline is the kitchen prep that determines your RAG system’s accuracy ceiling.
  • Tiny chunks cause “half-truth” hallucinations; giant chunks cause “semantic blur” via mean pooling.
  • Token limits like 512 tokens must be strictly respected to avoid silent data truncation.
  • Recursive and structure-aware splitting protect paragraphs, code blocks, and tables.

But what happens when documents don’t have neat headings?
What happens when you have messy meeting transcripts where people switch topics unpredictably?
And what happens when your vector search needs small chunks for search accuracy, but your LLM needs an entire 2-page policy for context?

In Part 5, we take chunking to the advanced level:

  • Bounded Semantic Chunking: Detecting topic shifts dynamically with mathematical distance thresholds and size guardrails.
  • Parent-Document Retrieval (Small-to-Big): How to search tiny child chunks while feeding large parent sections to the LLM (and how this prevents an $8,400 medical bill surprise!).
  • Breadcrumbs vs. Anthropic’s Contextual Retrieval: The complete architectural face-off.
  • The Production Decision Matrix: Choosing the exact strategy for your document types.

👉 Continue to Part 5: Advanced RAG Chunking: Hierarchical, Semantic, and Contextual Retrieval

What’s the trickiest chunking bug you’ve encountered in your own pipelines? Have you seen tables or severed sentences trip up your models? Let’s chat in the comments!

items.title: Delete Is a Promise: A Security Researcher’s Look at AI Conversation Privacy
items.summary: An OpenAI privacy bug in the gap between an object and the assets derived from it Summary When you share a ChatGPT conversation, the share page gets an Open Graph preview image served from a separate hostname. I found that deleting the conversation correctly invalidated the share page, but the preview image kept being served without authentication, with an excerpt of the deleted conversation still in it. I reported it to OpenAI through Bugcrowd. It was a duplicate of a report filed six days before mine, and the submission has since been marked resolved. Every test described here used my own account and my own conversations. I have left the real conversation IDs out of this post. Background: one share, two public URLs Creating a share link gives you a page at https://chatgpt.com/share/ . Chat apps and social networks fetch the page's Open Graph metadata to build a link preview. For a live share, that metadata describes the conversation, and the preview image comes from a different host: https://ogimg.chatgpt.com/conversation/ /response_multicolor_v1.png The same conversation ID appears in both URLs. The PNG contains an excerpt of the response text on a colored background. The image request carries no cookies and needs no login, which makes sense for a resource that crawlers fetch. So a single user action, sharing, produces two public surfaces. The question I wanted to answer was whether a single user action in the other direction, deleting, reaches both of them. Figure 1. Deleting the conversation was applied to the share page. The preview image kept returning the same bytes. The test The sequence was: Start a new conversation and create a share link with Share, then Create link. Fetch the share page and confirm its metadata reflects the conversation. Fetch the preview image URL and confirm the PNG contains conversation text. Record its checksum. Delete the conversation from the ChatGPT UI. Re-fetch the share page. Re-fetch the preview image, including with a cache-busting query parameter to rule out my own client cache. Compare checksums and response headers. The checks I ran, with the ID as a placeholder: ID=" " IMG="https://ogimg.chatgpt.com/conversation/$ID/response_multicolor_v1.png" # before deletion curl -s -D before.headers -o before.png "$IMG" md5sum before.png curl -s "https://chatgpt.com/share/$ID" | grep -i 'og:' # delete the conversation in the UI, then: curl -s -D after.headers -o after.png "$IMG?cb=$RANDOM" md5sum after.png head -n 1 after.headers grep -i -E '^(cache-control|age|access-control-allow-origin):' after.headers curl -s "https://chatgpt.com/share/$ID" | grep -i 'og:' What I observed After deletion, the share page stopped exposing conversation-specific metadata and fell back to generic defaults. The preview image still returned HTTP 200 with no authentication. The MD5 of the image was identical before and after deletion: 665c039d3d994998affa52b2835cba50. Same bytes, not a regenerated lookalike. The same hash came back about 5 minutes and about 26 minutes after deletion, including on a request with a cache-busting query parameter. The response headers were cache-control: public, max-age=86400, stale-while-revalidate=3600 and access-control-allow-origin: *. On September 5, more than 48 hours after deletion, the same URL still returned the same conversation-derived image. Cache or storage? This is the part where it is easy to overclaim, so here is what the evidence does and does not support. The response advertised max-age=86400 and stale-while-revalidate=3600. A cache that follows those headers can serve an entry as fresh for 24 hours after it was stored, then serve it stale for at most one more hour while it revalidates in the background. If the origin had stopped serving the image at deletion time, the longest a compliant shared cache could keep returning it is roughly 25 hours. I saw it at 48 hours or more. items.summary_html:
An OpenAI privacy bug in the gap between an object and the assets derived from itSummary

When you share a ChatGPT conversation, the share page gets an Open Graph preview image served from a separate hostname. I found that deleting the conversation correctly invalidated the share page, but the preview image kept being served without authentication, with an excerpt of the deleted conversation still in it.

I reported it to OpenAI through Bugcrowd. It was a duplicate of a report filed six days before mine, and the submission has since been marked resolved. Every test described here used my own account and my own conversations. I have left the real conversation IDs out of this post.

Background: one share, two public URLs

Creating a share link gives you a page at https://chatgpt.com/share/. Chat apps and social networks fetch the page's Open Graph metadata to build a link preview. For a live share, that metadata describes the conversation, and the preview image comes from a different host:

https://ogimg.chatgpt.com/conversation//response_multicolor_v1.png

The same conversation ID appears in both URLs. The PNG contains an excerpt of the response text on a colored background. The image request carries no cookies and needs no login, which makes sense for a resource that crawlers fetch.

So a single user action, sharing, produces two public surfaces. The question I wanted to answer was whether a single user action in the other direction, deleting, reaches both of them.

Figure 1. Deleting the conversation was applied to the share page. The preview image kept returning the same bytes.The test

The sequence was:

  1. Start a new conversation and create a share link with Share, then Create link.
  2. Fetch the share page and confirm its metadata reflects the conversation.
  3. Fetch the preview image URL and confirm the PNG contains conversation text. Record its checksum.
  4. Delete the conversation from the ChatGPT UI.
  5. Re-fetch the share page. Re-fetch the preview image, including with a cache-busting query parameter to rule out my own client cache.
  6. Compare checksums and response headers.

The checks I ran, with the ID as a placeholder:

ID=""
IMG="https://ogimg.chatgpt.com/conversation/$ID/response_multicolor_v1.png"

# before deletion
curl -s -D before.headers -o before.png "$IMG"
md5sum before.png
curl -s "https://chatgpt.com/share/$ID" | grep -i 'og:'

# delete the conversation in the UI, then:
curl -s -D after.headers -o after.png "$IMG?cb=$RANDOM"
md5sum after.png
head -n 1 after.headers
grep -i -E '^(cache-control|age|access-control-allow-origin):' after.headers
curl -s "https://chatgpt.com/share/$ID" | grep -i 'og:'
What I observed
  • After deletion, the share page stopped exposing conversation-specific metadata and fell back to generic defaults.
  • The preview image still returned HTTP 200 with no authentication.
  • The MD5 of the image was identical before and after deletion: 665c039d3d994998affa52b2835cba50. Same bytes, not a regenerated lookalike.
  • The same hash came back about 5 minutes and about 26 minutes after deletion, including on a request with a cache-busting query parameter.
  • The response headers were cache-control: public, max-age=86400, stale-while-revalidate=3600 and access-control-allow-origin: *.

On September 5, more than 48 hours after deletion, the same URL still returned the same conversation-derived image.

Cache or storage?

This is the part where it is easy to overclaim, so here is what the evidence does and does not support.

The response advertised max-age=86400 and stale-while-revalidate=3600. A cache that follows those headers can serve an entry as fresh for 24 hours after it was stored, then serve it stale for at most one more hour while it revalidates in the background. If the origin had stopped serving the image at deletion time, the longest a compliant shared cache could keep returning it is roughly 25 hours.

I saw it at 48 hours or more. That does not prove anything about OpenAI’s internals, since tiered caches and misconfigured caches exist, but it moves ordinary TTL expiry down the list of likely explanations.

Figure 2. Observations plotted against the lifetime the response headers advertised.

The cache-busting result narrows things too. Identical bytes on a request with a new query string means one of the following:

  • The cache key ignores the query string, so my parameter hit the same entry.
  • The generated image is stored in a backing store keyed by conversation ID, and the image service serves it without checking whether the source conversation or share still exists.
  • A cache layer is configured to serve stale content when the origin returns an error. If the origin answered with an error for a deleted conversation instead of a clean 404 or a placeholder, the cache could hide the deletion for much longer than the TTL suggests.

From the outside I cannot tell these apart, and my report said so. What I could establish was the externally observable behavior: a public, unauthenticated URL kept returning content derived from a deleted conversation for longer than the response headers would explain.

The fix that did not generalize

Later, the preview URL from my original test started returning a generic ChatGPT image. That looked like a remediation.

On September 30 I ran the whole sequence again with a brand new conversation. About 26 hours after deleting it, its preview image was still returning conversation-derived content. My reading, and it is only a reading, is that the first fix touched that specific asset rather than the deletion path. The report was moved back to Unresolved on October 4 and marked Resolved on October 6. I do not know what changed behind the scenes.

Figure 3. Report timeline.Impact, and why P4 is a fair rating

The triage team rated this P4, and I think that is reasonable. The limits are real:

  • You need the conversation ID, which is long and not guessable. I did not test enumeration and have no reason to think it works.
  • The image shows an excerpt, not the full conversation.
  • It only applies to conversations the owner had already chosen to share.

Who can still use it? Anyone who already held the link: the people it was sent to, anyone who saw it in a chat history, browser history or log, and anything that stored the URL. Those are exactly the people a user is trying to cut off when they delete a shared conversation after changing their mind or sharing with the wrong person.

There is also a layer OpenAI does not control. Messaging and social platforms that generate link previews often keep their own copy of the image. Deletion cannot reach those. That makes the origin and CDN the only layers where the vendor can actually enforce a delete, which is a good reason to get those right.

The behavior also conflicts with what the product says. OpenAI’s documentation states that deleting a conversation removes its shared link. A user reading that does not expect a second URL to keep the content reachable.

It was a duplicate

Bugcrowd marked my report as a duplicate of one submitted on August 28, six days before mine. No bounty, which is how duplicates work, and I do not mind it. The second reproduction after the first apparent fix is probably the most useful thing my report added.

What a fix looks like

This is a design sketch based on what I could observe, not a description of OpenAI’s system.

Figure 4. Deletion as a fan-out, with two backstops if a purge fails.
  1. Treat delete as a fan-out. When a feature creates a derived public asset, the same change should add a deletion hook for it. A list of derived assets per object type, reviewed when features ship, catches most of these.
  2. Purge by key, not by URL. Tag cached objects with the conversation ID so one purge covers every variant and every query string.
  3. Make the image endpoint check on a miss. If the share record is gone, return a generic placeholder or a 404. Do not rely on the generation step having been the last time anyone looked.
  4. Keep TTLs short for assets derived from deletable content. A max-age of one day is a deletion SLA of one day at best. ETag revalidation keeps the origin cost low.
  5. Do not fail open. Serving stale on origin errors is useful for availability and wrong for content a user has deleted.
Testing deletion in your own product

Checking that the main database row is gone is not enough. A lifecycle test looks like this:

  1. Create the object and share it.
  2. Collect every URL derived from it: the page, og:image, twitter:image, oEmbed endpoints, feeds, sitemaps, thumbnails.
  3. Fetch each one and store the hash and the headers.
  4. Delete the object.
  5. Re-fetch each URL with and without a changed query string at 5 minutes, 1 hour, just past your longest TTL, and 48 hours.
  6. Fail the test if any hash still matches the pre-delete content.

Step 5 with the changed query string is what separates a cache that is merely slow from a store that never got the delete.

Disclosure note

All testing was done against my own account and my own conversations. No other user’s data was accessed. The issue was reported through OpenAI’s Bugcrowd program, marked Resolved and Duplicate, and this post was coordinated through Bugcrowd’s disclosure process. Conversation IDs are omitted.

items.title: My RTX 5090 Fell from 77 to 7 Tokens Per Second. VRAM Pressure Was the Culprit
items.summary: A local LLM on a daily-driver Windows desktop. Every video call cut its speed by up to 10x, and vLLM never reported an error. The decisive test, the VRAM math, and the configuration change that stopped it. I run a 27B local model on my own desktop. Not a server, not a headless box: the same Windows 11 machine I take calls on and write on all day. It has an RTX 5090 with 32 GB of VRAM, vLLM running in WSL2, and it serves Qwen3.8 27B, NVFP4-quantized, to a DeepSeek Harness (DSH) agent that runs multi-hour coding sessions: shell, edits, tests, subagents, web search, and document work. This machine was one of three in a separate comparison I wrote up: DGX Spark, RTX 5090, Radeon R9700. The 5090 was the fastest of the three in long coding sessions. It was also the one that collapsed to single-digit tokens per second during each of three video calls. The part worth writing up is that nothing failed. vLLM never threw an out-of-memory error and never crashed. When the desktop needed VRAM, generation slowed to a fraction of its normal rate, and the token rate was the only sign . If you expect a GPU that runs out of memory to tell you so, this is the case where it didn’t. This is the diagnosis, end-to-end: the symptoms, the test that isolated the cause, the VRAM math, and the configuration change that stopped it. Every number is from that one machine and my workload. Where the evidence doesn’t fully close a question, I say so. The fix, in one table https://medium.com/media/dfb578e18753dcb85bb2700701dc8fc7/href The diagnostic that pointed at memory, separate from the fix: a short-request run stuck at 10–11 tok/s, with KV cache usage at 1.7%, returned to 82.8 tok/s after restarting only vLLM. The tok/s figures are observed DSH session rates and vLLM reporting intervals on this one machine, not a controlled benchmark. Below: how I got from “it’s slow” to that table. The symptoms The pattern was what first pointed me toward memory pressure rather than the model itself. One DSH session began around 77 tokens per second . By the end, the session average was around 27 , and that average includes the stretch at 77, so the late rate was far lower. A subagent running on the same server during the collapse measured around 7 . The agent never hung. It kept producing work, just slowly. That session overlapped two Teams calls, and each call brought a slowdown. Twice during Teams calls while the agent was running, the screen blacked out or flickered, Teams crashed, and the video failed on rejoining. The agent and the desktop were fighting over the same card. In troubleshooting, the card showed 32,049 MiB in use , nearly its entire 32 GB. The telemetry did not indicate thermal or power throttling. The card was not overheating. It was full. The decisive test After the second call caused the second slowdown, a short-request run had fallen to roughly 10–11 tokens per second . During that slow run, vLLM reported KV cache usage at just 1.7% . That number rules out KV-cache exhaustion. And because this was a short-request run, not a huge prefill, prompt length wasn’t a credible explanation either. Then I restarted only vLLM. Not the desktop. Not the model. Not the configuration. One process. The same run returned to 82.8 tokens per second . The restart doesn’t say which serving state was the problem. A fresh process reloads the weights and reallocates the cache, so it would fix either one. What it does say is that the model, the prompt, and the client were fine, and the serving process’s memory state was not. Then I took a third call with the configuration unchanged. Performance took a nose dive again. Call, collapse. Restart, recovery. Call, collapse. That sequence is the diagnosis: the trigger was the desktop’s GPU demand during calls, and what suffered was vLLM’s memory state. What was actually happening The flag at the center of it is ` — — gpu-memory-utilization`. It sets vLLM’s GPU memory budget for this instance : the share of the card that vLLM can treat as its own. I had it at 0.93 . On a 32 GB card, that leaves a little over 2 GB for everything else the card does: the Windows desktop, the display compositor, and Teams’ video encoding. That split is fine on a quiet desktop. It stops being fine the moment a video call actually uses the GPU. When the call added GPU demand, my working explanation is that some of vLLM’s allocations lost physical VRAM residency : pushed out of VRAM to make room for the desktop. Under WSL/Windows GPU memory management, that can mean data is served from system memory instead, introducing PCIe traffic into the decode path, which would explain a slowdown of this size. Stated as a ladder, because the levels matter: - Observed : the card is nearly full; a desktop workload is triggering the slowdown; a restart restores performance; low KV utilization rules out cache saturation; more headroom prevents the severe recurrence. - Strong inference: contention for physical VRAM is the failure mode. - Hypothesis: some serving allocation was evicted or migrated into host-visible memory, and the resulting PCIe traffic caused the token-rate loss. I did not trace any migration into system memory, and I did not isolate which allocations lost residency (weights, KV cache, or both). The PCIe detail is the rung that best fits the observations, not something I measured. I’m not going to pretend it is. The math: why 32 GB is the real constraint “The model fits” was never the issue; the model always fit. The question is how much VRAM remains after the model loads, because a model that fits in VRAM is not the same as a serving configuration with sufficient headroom. A 27B model at two bytes per parameter needs about 54 GB for weights alone in FP16/BF16, so on a 32 GB card, it has to be quantized. Two NVFP4 builds, measured in a 16,384-token judge setup: https://medium.com/media/ace08f0ae917c206091da3d1f707a489/href A note on the columns, because they look like they don’t add up: “Left for KV cache” is a hand calc, budget minus weights. vLLM doesn’t hand all of that to the cache; it first carves out a fixed chunk for activation and graph memory (roughly 1.5 GiB at these settings, as the two rows imply), and that fixed cost eats a larger share of the small Unsloth pool than of the ModelOpt one. The bytes per cached token are the same in both builds; what differs is how much of the leftover each pool actually gets. Those are configuration-specific cache capacities, not guaranteed context lengths. The ModelOpt build’s smaller weight footprint is why my long agent sessions have meaningful KV headroom at all, and the FP8 KV cache in my launch script halves the bytes per cached token on top of that. The issue was never the model. It was who keeps residency when the desktop competes for the same 32 GB , and at a 0.93 budget, there wasn’t enough headroom for the desktop and the serving process to coexist cleanly. The fix Two changes were made after the third call. 1. ` — — gpu-memory-utilization`: 0.93 → 0.85. This is the intervention aimed at desktop contention: give the card room to breathe for Windows and video calls, returning roughly 2.5 GiB to the desktop. 2. ` — — max-model-len`: 262,144 → 163,840. This is a workload guardrail, not a memory fix: it caps the length of a single request. To be clear about what it does not do: it does not give VRAM back to the desktop. The memory budget is the flag that does that. Both are precautions against the diagnosed memory-pressure failure mode. I changed them together, so I can’t attribute the result to either one alone. The fix has a price. The lower budget takes about 2.5 GiB away from vLLM, more than a quarter of the 9.26 GiB KV pool this build had in the judge setup, and the lower ceiling gives up about 98,000 tokens of maximum request length. For my workload (sustained agent sessions that compact as they run), that trade was worth it. Since making both changes, I have taken multiple Teams calls with the agent running and have not recreated the severe collapse. The worst drop I have seen since is roughly 83 to 52 tokens per second . Fair warning: the 5090 still has more throughput volatility in my use than the Spark or the Radeon. If you’re running vLLM on a desktop card Two things I would check. Budget VRAM for the desktop. If the card also drives your screen, ` — — gpu-memory-utilization` is a negotiation between the model and everything else on that card. A headless box can run hot; a desktop card can’t. Test under the load you actually run. This collapse showed up three times with a video call open, not during a quiet benchmark. If your desktop does anything that touches the GPU (video calls, second monitors, anything), test your serving rate while it's running. Reproduce it The launch script, sanitized: #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail # Initialize Conda for non-interactive shell source /path/to/miniconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh conda activate env_vllm export CUDA_HOME=/path/to/miniconda3/envs/env_vllm/lib/python3.12/site-packages/nvidia/cu13 export PATH="$CUDA_HOME/bin:$PATH" export LIBRARY_PATH="/usr/lib/wsl/lib:${LIBRARY_PATH:-}" export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 vllm serve \ gittensor-model-hub/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4-RTX5090 \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ --served-model-name qwen3.8-27b \ --seed 0 \ --tensor-parallel-size 1 \ --trust-remote-code \ --max-model-len 163840 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --max-num-seqs 2 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"preserve_thinking":false,"reasoning_effort":"medium"}' \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \ --generation-config vllm \ --override-generation-config '{ "temperature": 0.8, "top_k": 40, "top_p": 0.95, "min_p": 0.05, "repetition_penalty": 1.0 }' Two flags to change before you copy this. ` — — host 0.0.0.0` listens on every network interface with no API key, so bind to `127.0.0.1` (my agent connects over loopback) or add ` — — api-key` if anything else on your network can reach the machine. And ` — — trust-remote-code` runs code shipped with the checkpoint, so know what you’re trusting. `env_vllm` is a pinned conda environment ( Python 3.12.14, vLLM 0.29.0, torch 2.13.0+cu130 ), rebuilt from an environment file and a requirements lock exported from the working machine. The `CUDA_HOME` and `PATH` exports put that environment’s own CUDA toolkit on the load path, `LIBRARY_PATH` is the WSL piece, and `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` pins the non-v2 model runner. The checkpoint is the 5090-oriented NVFP4 build . Its model card notes that the MTP head was removed, so the script doesn’t enable speculative decoding. If you serve a different build, such as the Unsloth NVFP4 checkpoint , re-run the headroom math before you trust my numbers. Bottom line A 32 GB card shared with a desktop is a negotiation. At a 0.93 vLLM budget, mine crossed the line three times without vLLM ever reporting an error. Dropping the budget to 0.85 gave Windows enough headroom that I haven’t reproduced the severe collapse since. The caveats, because they’re the difference between a field report and a press release: one machine, one workload, my measurements, and no isolation of which serving state left the card. This post is the VRAM diagnosis from my three-platform comparison , One Harness, One Agent, Three GPUs: Running Qwen on a DGX Spark, an RTX 5090, and a Radeon R9700 . In that comparison, the 5090 was the fastest of the three in long coding sessions. The fix above is what kept that speed from turning into a black screen mid-call. My RTX 5090 Fell from 77 to 7 Tokens Per Second. VRAM Pressure Was the Culprit was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Stated as a ladder, because the levels matter:

- Strong inference: contention for physical VRAM is the failure mode.
- Hypothesis: some serving allocation was evicted or migrated into host-visible memory, and the resulting PCIe traffic caused the token-rate loss.

I did not trace any migration into system memory, and I did not isolate which allocations lost residency (weights, KV cache, or both). The PCIe detail is the rung that best fits the observations, not something I measured. I’m not going to pretend it is.

The math: why 32 GB is the real constraint

“The model fits” was never the issue; the model always fit. The question is how much VRAM remains after the model loads, because a model that fits in VRAM is not the same as a serving configuration with sufficient headroom. A 27B model at two bytes per parameter needs about 54 GB for weights alone in FP16/BF16, so on a 32 GB card, it has to be quantized.

Two NVFP4 builds, measured in a 16,384-token judge setup:

https://medium.com/media/ace08f0ae917c206091da3d1f707a489/href

A note on the columns, because they look like they don’t add up: “Left for KV cache” is a hand calc, budget minus weights. vLLM doesn’t hand all of that to the cache; it first carves out a fixed chunk for activation and graph memory (roughly 1.5 GiB at these settings, as the two rows imply), and that fixed cost eats a larger share of the small Unsloth pool than of the ModelOpt one. The bytes per cached token are the same in both builds; what differs is how much of the leftover each pool actually gets.

Those are configuration-specific cache capacities, not guaranteed context lengths. The ModelOpt build’s smaller weight footprint is why my long agent sessions have meaningful KV headroom at all, and the FP8 KV cache in my launch script halves the bytes per cached token on top of that.

The issue was never the model. It was who keeps residency when the desktop competes for the same 32 GB, and at a 0.93 budget, there wasn’t enough headroom for the desktop and the serving process to coexist cleanly.

The fix

Two changes were made after the third call.

1. ` — — gpu-memory-utilization`: 0.93 → 0.85. This is the intervention aimed at desktop contention: give the card room to breathe for Windows and video calls, returning roughly 2.5 GiB to the desktop.
2. ` — — max-model-len`: 262,144 → 163,840. This is a workload guardrail, not a memory fix: it caps the length of a single request. To be clear about what it does not do: it does not give VRAM back to the desktop. The memory budget is the flag that does that.

Both are precautions against the diagnosed memory-pressure failure mode. I changed them together, so I can’t attribute the result to either one alone.

The fix has a price. The lower budget takes about 2.5 GiB away from vLLM, more than a quarter of the 9.26 GiB KV pool this build had in the judge setup, and the lower ceiling gives up about 98,000 tokens of maximum request length. For my workload (sustained agent sessions that compact as they run), that trade was worth it.

Since making both changes, I have taken multiple Teams calls with the agent running and have not recreated the severe collapse. The worst drop I have seen since is roughly 83 to 52 tokens per second. Fair warning: the 5090 still has more throughput volatility in my use than the Spark or the Radeon.

If you’re running vLLM on a desktop card

Two things I would check.

  1. Budget VRAM for the desktop. If the card also drives your screen, ` — — gpu-memory-utilization` is a negotiation between the model and everything else on that card. A headless box can run hot; a desktop card can’t.
  2. Test under the load you actually run. This collapse showed up three times with a video call open, not during a quiet benchmark. If your desktop does anything that touches the GPU (video calls, second monitors, anything), test your serving rate while it's running.
Reproduce it

The launch script, sanitized:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Initialize Conda for non-interactive shell
source /path/to/miniconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
conda activate env_vllm

export CUDA_HOME=/path/to/miniconda3/envs/env_vllm/lib/python3.12/site-packages/nvidia/cu13
export PATH="$CUDA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export LIBRARY_PATH="/usr/lib/wsl/lib:${LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0

vllm serve \
  gittensor-model-hub/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4-RTX5090 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  --served-model-name qwen3.8-27b \
  --seed 0 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --max-model-len 163840 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --max-num-seqs 2 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"preserve_thinking":false,"reasoning_effort":"medium"}' \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \
  --generation-config vllm \
  --override-generation-config '{
    "temperature": 0.8,
    "top_k": 40,
    "top_p": 0.95,
    "min_p": 0.05,
    "repetition_penalty": 1.0
  }'

Two flags to change before you copy this. ` — — host 0.0.0.0` listens on every network interface with no API key, so bind to `127.0.0.1` (my agent connects over loopback) or add ` — — api-key` if anything else on your network can reach the machine. And ` — — trust-remote-code` runs code shipped with the checkpoint, so know what you’re trusting.

`env_vllm` is a pinned conda environment (Python 3.12.14, vLLM 0.29.0, torch 2.13.0+cu130), rebuilt from an environment file and a requirements lock exported from the working machine. The `CUDA_HOME` and `PATH` exports put that environment’s own CUDA toolkit on the load path, `LIBRARY_PATH` is the WSL piece, and `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` pins the non-v2 model runner.

The checkpoint is the 5090-oriented NVFP4 build. Its model card notes that the MTP head was removed, so the script doesn’t enable speculative decoding. If you serve a different build, such as the Unsloth NVFP4 checkpoint, re-run the headroom math before you trust my numbers.

Bottom line

A 32 GB card shared with a desktop is a negotiation. At a 0.93 vLLM budget, mine crossed the line three times without vLLM ever reporting an error. Dropping the budget to 0.85 gave Windows enough headroom that I haven’t reproduced the severe collapse since.

The caveats, because they’re the difference between a field report and a press release: one machine, one workload, my measurements, and no isolation of which serving state left the card.

This post is the VRAM diagnosis from my three-platform comparison, One Harness, One Agent, Three GPUs: Running Qwen on a DGX Spark, an RTX 5090, and a Radeon R9700. In that comparison, the 5090 was the fastest of the three in long coding sessions. The fix above is what kept that speed from turning into a black screen mid-call.

items.title: How Does AI Game Merging Actually Work?
items.summary: Cross-game clips can look like a new engine, but the build may be a content port, a bridge between two running games, or a rebuilt runtime. Each route moves a different layer — and proves a different thing. AI Game Merging｜Generated by ChatGPT Some clips make it look as if one game has swallowed another. In practice, a clean frame doesn’t reveal whether it came from a small mechanic port, two games connected by a bridge, or a rebuilt runtime. The agent may help write the glue; it doesn’t erase the differences between the games. The question has become harder to ignore. A Numerama report published October 2, 2026 describes new mashup clips appearing on social feeds from September 29 onward. But the clips do not all disclose whether AI was used, and a report about a trend is not proof of how any one project works. If you watched a game-mashup video and want to know what “merge” means under the hood, look for what is running, what crosses between games, and what the demo actually tested . Those three questions separate the engineering from the spectacle. “Merging” describes the result, not the method A game mashup can look unified while its implementation stays split. A character, weapon, block, or rule from one game appears inside another. That does not tell you whether the guest game is still running, whether its code was rewritten, or whether the host simply imitates one mechanic. The distinction matters because each approach changes a different layer. A mechanic port changes the host game’s content. A passthrough mod links two running game processes. A reimplementation builds a new runtime or simulation for some part of the guest game. All three can produce a compelling clip, but they don’t carry the same amount of the original game with them. Same screen, different systems. Think of “Minecraft inside GTA” as a question, not an architecture diagram. Is Minecraft running beside GTA? Are Minecraft’s rules recreated as GTA-native behavior? Or is a new Minecraft-like runtime being drawn into GTA? A video title doesn’t answer that. A clip shows the output. The route explains what was actually merged. Three Routes for AI Game Merging A mechanic port makes the host own the new rule In a content port, the host game runs the borrowed behavior through its own mod system. The Universal Modder mashup guide describes adding an enemy, weapon, or block as new host content that imitates the guest. A creeper-like enemy in another game, for example, can use that game’s AI state machine and projectile system. The host owns the behavior This route doesn’t need the guest game to run. The modder studies the guest mechanic — its speed, damage, timing, or state changes — then expresses that behavior in the host’s API. The host remains responsible for animation, collision, save behavior, and whatever rules its engine expects. One host, one borrowed mechanic. That makes a mechanic port lighter than synchronizing two full simulations. It can also change the feel. A copied movement rule may behave differently under the host’s gravity, frame timing, or collision model. The borrowed idea can be recognizable without being bit-for-bit identical to the guest; it isn’t the guest’s full simulation. Assets are a separate problem from behavior. The project guide advises using converters on the player’s own installation or making new lookalikes instead of placing another game’s files in a mod. A visually similar sprite doesn’t prove that the original asset or code was transferred — and a technically working port doesn’t settle what may be redistributed. Passthrough keeps both games running A passthrough mod links two live processes instead of asking one engine to become the other. Each game keeps much of its own simulation, while adapters exchange selected information such as position, camera, collision, input, or events. Rendering code then makes the guest’s output fit into the host’s scene. The documented Minecraft × GTA V example makes that concrete. A Fabric mod runs Minecraft alongside GTA V story mode. GTA sends its camera and nearby ground across a local WebSocket; Minecraft sends color and depth frames through shared memory; a ReShade add-on composites those frames against GTA’s depth buffer. Events such as Minecraft explosions can also trigger corresponding GTA effects. The synchronization is the hard part hiding behind the clip. The two games use different coordinate systems, clocks, collision rules, and render pipelines. The project maps GTA’s coordinates into Minecraft’s, feeds nearby ground back as blocks, and reprojects a slightly delayed frame so it follows GTA’s current camera. The example README documents a specific GTA V Legacy and Minecraft Java setup; it is evidence about that pairing, not a plug-and-play recipe for every pair of games. Passthrough is useful when keeping the guest’s real simulation matters. It also creates more seams to test: message timing, frame delay, collision feedback, and what happens when one process stalls. If the goal only needs a guest weapon or enemy, running a second game may add needless complexity; it doesn’t automatically make the merge more complete. The bridge is where the friction appears Reimplementation rebuilds part of the guest A reimplementation replaces a guest runtime — or its rules — with a new piece of software. Instead of launching the original guest game, a project can rebuild an engine or a focused simulation that reads data from the player’s own copy, then connect that new runtime to a host. The Universal Modder guide presents this as a heavier route with more control; it also describes headless rule simulations where the host remains the view. This isn’t the same as “copy the game into the other game.” Code has to be reconstructed or rewritten, data formats understood, and the new runtime’s timing and coordinate assumptions made compatible with the host. A rebuilt engine may preserve more behavior than a hand-written mechanic port, but it can still diverge at edge cases. A headless simulation can be much narrower: it may reproduce the guest’s rules without reproducing its renderer, menus, or every system around them. The project documentation also lists embedding a decompiled game as a library as its own pattern. That can reuse an existing simulation rather than rebuild it, but the host still has to feed it inputs or collision and consume the returned state. So the three routes here are a reader’s map, not the repository’s full taxonomy. The AI agent helps with the workflow, not the merge itself The agent is one layer in a toolchain; the game-specific bridge is another. The Universal Modder repository describes a workflow that searches prior notes, identifies the engine, chooses a route, reads code, builds a small working slice, creates assets, tests in the actual game, and records what it learned. That workflow can make unfamiliar tools easier to coordinate. It doesn’t make two engines share a renderer, clock, coordinate system, or mod loader. Someone still has to choose a compatible pair, define which state crosses the boundary, decide what counts as a working result, and inspect the behavior in the target version. Recent coverage connects AI coding agents with this wave of mashups, but that link needs care. Numerama notes that creators do not all say whether AI was involved. The public project documents its own tools and examples; it does not establish that every widely shared clip used Universal Modder or an AI agent at all. Treat “AI-made” as a claim that needs project-specific evidence. Three questions tell you what a demo proves A short clip can prove that one visible path worked in one recorded setup. It cannot, by itself, prove that both games’ full systems were combined, that the project works across versions, or that it is stable enough for a long play session. Before repeating “AI merged two games,” check: What is running? Two original game processes, one host with new content, or a rebuilt guest runtime? What crosses the boundary? Position, camera, collision, input, events, rendered frames — or only an imitation of one rule? What was verified? A staged clip, a tested interaction, a versioned project note, or sustained play across more than one setup? Those answers turn a visual mashup into a technical claim you can evaluate. The right explanation may be “one mechanic was ported,” “two games were synchronized,” or “a guest runtime was rebuilt and fused.” Each is impressive for a different reason. The video is the doorway; the implementation path is the story. How Does AI Game Merging Actually Work? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: OpenAI came to Australia to apologise. It will leave without answering these key questions | Toby Walsh
items.summary: We don’t accept drugs killing a few people because they cure most patients. Or a few planes crashing because most land safely. AI should be no different OpenAI’s CEO Sam Altman was asked to appear before the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Australia and explain how and why their agents have been hacking into multiple government websites . Altman didn’t turn up but sent Jason Kwon, his chief strategy officer, instead to answer the committee’s many tricky questions on its first day of public hearings on Tuesday. The committee is conducting a comprehensive inquiry into the economic, societal, regulatory, and national security implications of AI for Australia. It will report back to parliament at the end of November. This is an unusually fast pace, but then it’s an unusually fast paced technology.
